paragraphs.text: In the year 1866, something remarkable happened at sea, a mysterious and baffling phenomenon. Although sailors were especially excited about it, the general public—even those who lived far inland—heard the rumors too. For some time vessels had been encountering "an enormous thing" at sea. This thing was a long, spindle-shaped object. People said it occasionally glowed, and it was larger and more rapid in its movements than any whale.

On July 20 the steamship Governor Higginson met the thing five miles off the east coast of Australia. At first Captain Baker thought he was in the presence of an unknown sandbank. He was about to determine its exact position in the ocean when two columns of water shot a hundred and fifty feet into the air with a loud hissing noise.

Three days later another ship spotted the thing—but this ship was fifteen hundred miles away in the Pacific! Fifteen days later and two thousand miles away, two more ships encountered the mysterious object.

Everyone began talking about the thing. They sang about it in the cafes, ridiculed it in the newspapers, and showcased it on the stage. All kinds of stories circulated about the object, causing editors of scientific journals to quarrel with believers in the supernatural. The subject was debated for six months until a journal poked such fun at the topic that stories about the strange thing finally died.

The topic seemed buried forever. But during the first months of 1867, new facts came to light. Suddenly the thing at sea was no longer a scientific problem to be solved but a real danger to be avoided.

On March 5, 1867, a Canadian passenger ship, the Moravian , struck a rock that wasn't marked on any map for that part of the Atlantic Ocean. Had it not been for the ship's superior strength, the Moravian would have gone down with all 237 passengers onboard.

The accident happened just as day was breaking. The officers rushed to the rear of the ship and carefully studied the sea. But they saw nothing except the surface of the water violently swirling about 1800 feet away. The exact location of the place was noted, and the Moravian continued on its route without apparent damage. Had it struck a rock or an enormous shipwreck? The ship’s officers had no idea. But when the ship’s bottom was examined while undergoing repairs, workers found that part of the keel was broken.

This incident might have been forgotten if the same thing hadn't happened a little more than a month later. Only in this case, the event caused a huge uproar because of the excellent reputation of the shipping line involved—the famous Cunard line of England. In 26 years Cunard ships had successfully made two thousand Atlantic crossings without a voyage canceled, a delay recorded, or a man, a ship, or even a letter lost.
On April 13, 1867, with a smooth sea and a moderate breeze, the Cunard’s Scotia was crossing the Atlantic, headed for England.
At a little after four o’clock in the afternoon, while the passengers were having tea, a slight shock was felt. The Scotia had not struck anything; instead it had been struck.
The shock had been so slight that no one was alarmed at first. But then a member of the crew started shouting, "We're sinking! We're sinking!"

The passengers were very afraid, so Captain Anderson quickly reassured them that the ship was not in danger of sinking. The Scotia , divided into seven compartments by strong partitions, could withstand any leak. Captain Anderson soon found that the sea was rapidly pouring into the fifth compartment. He ordered the engines to be stopped at once, and one of the men dove into the water to determine the damage. He found a large hole, two yards in diameter.

Such a leak could not be stopped, so the Scotia was forced to continue on its way. The ship was then about three hundred miles from Ireland, and after three days’ delay, it finally reached a British port. When the Scotia was examined more carefully, the hole was found to be in the shape of a triangle. Something had punched its way through the ship’s thick iron plates and then pulled out.
From this moment on, the monster was blamed for any accident at sea.

During the time that these developments were taking place, I was returning from a scientific expedition to explore the Nebraska Territory in the United States. The French government had sent me, Pierre Aronnax, on the expedition because I am an assistant professor at the Museum of Natural History in Paris. After six months in Nebraska, I had arrived in New York City with a precious collection of minerals, plants, and animals. I was not due to return to France for a while, so I was busy organizing my specimens when the Scotia incident occurred.

I was well aware of this unfortunate event and the debate over its cause. How could I not have been? I had read and reread every American and European newspaper without being able to form a conclusion. Something was out there; that much was certain.

While I was in New York, the issue reached a boiling point. People had discussed a theory about a drifting island or reef, but that idea had been completely eliminated. How could an island or reef move at such fantastic speed unless it had an engine in its belly?

For the same reason, the idea of a massive, floating shipwreck had also been abandoned. There were only two possible explanations for the thing, and each explanation had its supporters. On one side were those who were sure it was a monster of colossal strength. On the other side were those who believed the thing was some type of underwater boat with tremendous engine power.
But this second idea seemed nearly impossible. How could a private individual have a vessel like this at his command? Where had it been built, and how had its construction been kept secret?

It was possible, however, that a nation might construct a submarine to use as a weapon of war. But rival countries are always watching each other. It was unlikely that one nation could have built a submarine without another nation knowing about it. Inquiries were made in England, France, Russia, Prussia, Spain, Italy, America, and even in Turkey. When the inquiries produced no facts, the hypothesis of a submarine was rejected.

And so the idea of a monster surfaced again. Upon my arrival in New York, several people did me the honor of consulting me on the subject. In France I had published a two-volume work, Mysteries of the Great Underwater World . Well-regarded in academic circles, my book gave me a reputation as an expert in this obscure branch of natural history. By the time the New York Herald asked me to write an article on the subject, I had my own ideas about this monster.
As I wrote in my New York Herald article, there was only one good explanation for those mysterious events at sea: a marine animal of enormous power.

"The great depths of the sea are entirely unknown to us," I wrote in the newspaper. "Who knows what creatures live twelve or fifteen miles below the surface of the ocean? There is, however, one known animal powerful enough to pierce the hull of a steamship. The common narwhal, or sea unicorn, often grows to a length of sixty feet. Increase its size by five or ten times and you have a gigantic beast capable of causing great damage."

The ordinary narwhal is armed with an ivory tusk as hard as steel. Some of these tusks have killed whales and penetrated ships' hulls. One Paris museum possesses a narwhal tusk that is fifteen inches wide at its base and almost seven feet long. Now suppose that this tusk were six times stronger than usual and the animal ten times more powerful. Launch this weapon at high speed, and you would have a force capable of producing a catastrophe at sea.

"Until I receive more information," I concluded in my newspaper article, "I believe that the beast is a narwhal of colossal dimensions. Unless, of course, it's something above and beyond anything that anyone has ever seen or imagined."

I realized that I was undercutting my argument with this last sentence. But I wanted to protect my reputation as a distinguished professor and not give the Americans any more reasons to laugh at me. After all, I had just admitted that I believed in a sea monster.

My article was very popular, and soon everyone seemed to have an opinion about the gigantic narwhal. I still thought that it could exist. If huge dinosaurs had once roamed the earth, why couldn't an equally large narwhal cruise the seas?

Some people saw the creature's existence as a purely scientific problem. But more practical people, especially in England and the United States, were determined to rid the ocean of this beast. The sea must be made safe for travelers.

The United States led the way in this effort. In New York preparations were made for an expedition to pursue the narwhal. The warship Abraham Lincoln was armed and ready to depart under the command of Captain Farragut. But as soon as it was decided to go after the narwhal, the creature disappeared! For two months no ship encountered it. No one knew where to look for it. The Abraham Lincoln remained at the pier in Brooklyn.

Suddenly on June 2, a steamship on its way from California to Shanghai reported that it had seen the animal three weeks earlier in the northern part of the Pacific Ocean. Everyone was extremely excited. Captain Farragut did not want to waste another minute. The Abraham Lincoln was quickly stocked with food and coal, and I soon received the following letter at my New York hotel:
Dear Professor Aronnax:

The government of the United States invites you to join the Abraham Lincoln expedition as a representative from France. Captain Farragut will provide a cabin for your use during the expedition. The ship will be departing in three hours.
Very cordially yours,
J.B. Hobson
Secretary of the U.S. Navy
Three seconds before this letter arrived, I had no intention of pursuing the gigantic narwhal. Three seconds after it arrived, I felt my whole purpose in life was to chase down this creature.

I was still tired from my long trip to Nebraska. I wanted nothing more than to see my country, my friends, and my little apartment near the botanical gardens. But nothing could hold me back. I forgot everything—fatigue, friends, and home—and accepted without hesitation the offer from the American government.
"Conseil!" I called in an impatient voice.

Conseil was my servant, who had accompanied me on all my travels. I liked him and he liked me too. For the last ten years, Conseil, whose name means advice in French, had followed me wherever science had led me. Not once did he complain about the length of any journey. He was ready to pack his suitcase—and mine—for wherever we might be headed, whether to China or the Congo.

Conseil was a quiet young man, never upset by any surprises that life threw our way, and adept at any task required of him. He had even become an expert in putting plants and animals into their scientific classes. At the age of thirty, he was ten years younger than I.
"Conseil!" I called again as I began my feverish preparations for the journey.
I usually didn't ask if it were convenient for him to accompany me, but this expedition could be hazardous.
"Conseil!" I called a third time.
"Did you call me?" he asked, entering the room.
"Yes," I replied. "Pack up all our things; we're leaving in two hours. There's not a moment to lose."
"And what about your collections—the fossils and animal skins?"
"The hotel will take care of them for us," I said.
"And your live wild Indonesian swine?"
"Someone at the hotel will feed it during our absence," I answered. "I will give orders to forward everything to France."
"We're not returning to Paris?"
"Eventually." I outlined our expedition on the Abraham Lincoln and asked if he wished to accompany me this time.
"Whatever you do, Master, I'll do," Conseil replied.
I urged him to think over his decision. "There's an element of danger," I said. "This is one of those trips that people don't always survive."
"Whatever you wish," Conseil said calmly.

He soon had our bags packed, and we settled our hotel bill. I left instructions for shipping my containers of stuffed animals and dried plants to Paris. I arranged for the purchase of supplies for the care of my swine, and with Conseil at my heels, I jumped into a cab.

At the dock in Brooklyn, our luggage was immediately taken to the deck of the Abraham Lincoln . We hurried onboard and I asked for Captain Farragut. One of the sailors led me to a small deck on the stern of the ship. A handsome officer held out his hand to me. "Professor Pierre Aronnax?" he said.
"Yes, and you must be Captain Farragut."
The officer nodded. "Welcome, Professor. Your cabin is ready for you."

I let Conseil stow away our luggage while I watched Captain Farragut give the orders for the ship to cast off. A few minutes later and we would have missed the boat! The Abraham Lincoln moved majestically away from the pier. The docks on both sides of the East River were crowded with spectators. Half a million people cheered and waved their handkerchiefs as the warship moved down the river, toward the harbor.
By nightfall we had left the lights of the city behind and were running at full steam into the dark waters of the Atlantic.

Captain Farragut was a good seaman, worthy of the fine ship that he commanded. He believed in the gigantic narwhal and would not let anyone onboard question its existence. The creature was real, and he had sworn to rid the seas of it. Either Captain Farragut would kill the narwhal, or the narwhal would kill Captain Farragut. There was no third option.

The officers onboard the Abraham Lincoln shared their captain's opinion. They constantly discussed the narwhal, calculating the chances of meeting it. As for the crew, they wanted nothing more than to hunt down the sea unicorn, harpoon it, and hoist it onboard.

To add to the excitement, Captain Farragut offered a reward of two thousand dollars to the first man who spotted the creature. All eyes—including mine—were on the sea. Only one person onboard was indifferent to the chase and the reward, and that was Conseil.

Captain Farragut had provided his ship with everything necessary to catch the gigantic narwhal. No whaling ship had ever been better equipped. But the Abraham Lincoln 's best asset was Ned Land, the king of harpooners. Ned had been born in Canada forty years ago. Quick, cool, and cunning, he had no equal with the harpoon. Originally from Quebec, the French-speaking part of Canada, Ned took a liking to me. Little by little, this quiet man and I got to know each other quite well. I loved to hear him tell of his adventures on the ocean.

So what was his opinion on the question of the marine monster? I suspected that he did not believe in the sea unicorn. By the end of June, we had crossed the Atlantic and would soon reach Cape Horn at the southern tip of South America. Sitting on the deck with Ned, I led the conversation around to the topic of the gigantic narwhal. I examined the chances of success for our mission.
"But you don't believe in the existence of this creature, do you?" I said. "Is there any particular reason for that?"
The harpooner stared at me for a few moments before answering. "Perhaps there is, Professor Aronnax."
"But, Ned, you're a whaler by profession, familiar with all the great marine mammals. You should be the last person to doubt its existence."

"As a whaler, I've followed many large sea creatures and harpooned a great number of them," he said. "But no matter how strong they were, neither their tails nor their tusks could have even scratched the iron plates of a steamship."
I pointed out that there were reports of ships' hulls being pierced by the tusks of narwhals.

"Wooden ships," Ned said carefully. "That might be possible, though I've never seen it happen. So until I have further proof, I refuse to believe that whales or sea unicorns could ever produce the effect you describe."

I told him my theory that the creature might have come from unknown depths in the sea. Using mathematical equations, I explained how water pressure increases as water gets deeper. "Its body would have to be strong enough to resist water pressure equal to tens of millions of pounds."
"Then this creature must be made of iron plates that are eight inches thick, like an armored warship!" exclaimed Ned.
"Think what destruction such a creature would cause if it hurled itself against a ship's hull at the speed of an express train."
"Yes, well . . . perhaps," Ned replied, shaken by these thoughts but not yet willing to give in.
"So have I convinced you that such a creature exists?" I asked.
"You've convinced me of one thing: that if this animal lives at the bottom of the sea, it must be as strong as you say."
"But if it doesn't exist, how do you explain what happened to the Scotia ?"
"It . . ." Ned hesitated and then blurted out, "I explain it by pronouncing my conviction that it just couldn't be true!"

I stopped trying to convince Ned. Our ship sailed around Cape Horn and on to the Pacific. By the end of July we had reached the northern Pacific, where the creature was last reported. The entire ship's crew was full of nervous excitement. They could not eat; they could not sleep. Twenty times a day someone thought he spotted our prey.

For three more months the Abraham Lincoln sailed the waters of the northern Pacific. The days seemed to last forever as we explored every part of the ocean between Japan and North America. We found nothing.

No ship's crew had ever worked harder; the men did everything they could to find the gigantic narwhal. But now the crew members were calling themselves fools for believing in such a creature. Every man wanted to catch up on his eating and sleeping, to make up for the time he had so stupidly sacrificed. There was only one thing left to do: go home.

The men took this demand to Captain Farragut, but he refused to abandon the search. I won't say that they threatened to mutiny, but after their appeal to Farragut, they didn't perform their duties as well as they could have. At last Captain Farragut said that if the creature did not appear within three days, the pilot would turn the ship's wheel toward home.

Captain Farragut made this promise on November 2, and it rallied the crew. Everyone watched the ocean with renewed attention. Two days passed during which a thousand schemes were tried to attract the creature. Large quantities of bacon were trailed behind the ship, but that only succeeded in drawing sharks. When the ship stopped, men went out in small boats to continue their search. But November 4 arrived, and still the creature had not made an appearance. The deadline would expire at noon the next day.

Night was approaching. Large clouds veiled the face of the moon. The sea rocked gently under the stern of the vessel. At that moment I was leaning over the railing. Conseil, standing near me, was looking straight ahead. The crew, perched in the rigging, was scanning the horizon in the growing darkness.
"Come, Conseil," I said. "This is your last chance to earn the two thousand dollars."
"If you will permit me to say this, I never counted on getting the prize."
"You were right, Conseil," I admitted. "This was a foolish affair after all. We should have returned to France months ago."

"You would be in your little apartment and in the museum," replied Conseil. "I would have already classified all of your fossils. And the wild swine would have been drawing crowds to its cage at the zoo in the botanical gardens."
"You're right. We'll be laughed at for this adventure."
"That's for sure," Conseil said quietly. "I think people will make fun of you. And I hope you don't mind my saying so, Master, but you deserve it."
"What!"
"You're a very smart man, so you shouldn't expose yourself to—"
Just then someone started shouting. It was Ned Land.
"Look! Over there!" cried Ned. "It's the very thing we've been searching for!"

At Ned’s cry, everyone onboard the Abraham Lincoln rushed to get a look at the creature. Captain Farragut gave the order for the ship to stop. It was quite dark by then, so I wondered how Ned had been able to spot anything in the water. But he had not been mistaken because we could all see the object that he was pointing to.

About twelve hundred feet away, the sea seemed to be glowing. The creature gave off the intense mysterious light that several ships’ captains had mentioned in their reports. The immense oval of light condensed at the center into a blazing core.
"Oh, that’s only some phosphorescent sea animals," one officer said.
"No, sir, certainly not," I replied. "No sea animal ever produced such a powerful light; it’s almost like an electric light. Besides, that creature is headed straight for us!"
A cry of alarm went up from the ship.
"Silence!" roared Captain Farragut. "Reverse the engines."

Our ship moved away from the burning light, but the supernatural animal came after us at twice our speed. Everyone gasped. More surprised than fearful, we stood there unable to speak or move. The animal gained on us and circled the ship. Then it moved two or three miles away, trailing a glowing wake.

Suddenly the creature rushed toward the Abraham Lincoln at an alarming rate of speed. It stopped about twenty feet from our hull and the light died out. The animal reappeared on the other side of the vessel as if it had slid under our hull. At any moment a fatal collision might have occurred. But instead of attacking the creature, we fled—a maneuver that amazed me. Usually Captain Farragut displayed no emotion, but at that point he looked completely astonished.

"Professor Aronnax, I don’t know what kind of formidable creature I’m dealing with," he said as if he sensed that I was questioning his actions. "I won’t risk my ship in this darkness. Besides, how can we attack this unknown thing when we can’t see it? How can we defend ourselves from it? We must wait for daylight to attack this extraordinary narwhal."

The crew members of the Abraham Lincoln were on their feet all night. No one thought of sleep even though the ship slowed down. Imitating the warship, the creature let the waves rock it, but it seemed oddly determined not to leave the scene. Toward midnight, however, it disappeared, seeming to have died out like some large glowworm. Had it fled?
At about one o’clock in the morning, we heard a deafening whistle like that produced by water rushing with great force.
The captain, Ned, and I were on the small deck at the stern of the ship, eagerly peering through the darkness.
"Ned Land," said Captain Farragut, "you’ve often heard the roaring of whales, haven’t you?"
"Yes, sir, but never a whale like this. If only I could get close enough to harpoon it."
"But to approach it, you’d need a small boat," said the captain, "and that would risk the lives of my men."
"And my life too," Ned said quietly.

Toward two o’clock in the morning, the bright light reappeared about five miles away. Despite the distance and the noise of the wind and the sea, we distinctly heard the loud sounds as the animal beat the surface of the water with its tail. You could even hear its panting breath.

We were on the alert and prepared for combat. While one of the officers loaded weapons, Ned contented himself with sharpening his harpoon. At six o’clock, day began to break; with the first glimmer of daylight, the beast's bright light disappeared. At seven o’clock, a very thick fog obscured our view, and the best telescopes could not penetrate it. That caused much disappointment and anger onboard the ship.
I started to climb one of the masts; some of the officers were already above me. At eight o’clock, the fog began to lift.
Suddenly Ned cried out, "Look! There it is!"

Everyone turned toward where he pointed. A mile and a half from the ship, a long black body emerged a yard above the waves. The ship approached the beast and I examined it thoroughly. Prior reports had exaggerated its size; I estimated it to be no more than two hundred and fifty feet in length. While I observed the creature, it ejected two plumes of steam and water that reached a height of one hundred and twenty feet. So that was how it breathed! I concluded that it must be a sea mammal of some kind, although one that was electric, like an electric eel.
At last the moment for combat had arrived.

Captain Farragut gave his orders, and the Abraham Lincoln went straight at the animal. The beast allowed the ship to come within three hundred feet. Then as if refusing to dive, it made a little turn and stopped. We pursued the creature like this for almost an hour without gaining a yard on it.
"Well, Mr. Land," said the captain at last, "do you advise me to send out the small boats to capture the beast?"
"No, sir, because we won’t take this beast easily," replied Ned. "Increase our speed if you can, sir. I'll stand at the bow and throw my harpoon if I get the chance."

The Abraham Lincoln sped up to eighteen and a half miles per hour, but the animal swam at that speed too. For a whole hour, the ship kept up this pace without gaining on the beast. We increased our speed to above nineteen miles an hour, and so did the creature.
"We will catch it!" cried Ned as the animal let us get a little closer.

But just as Ned was about to throw his harpoon, the animal slipped away at a speed that was no less than thirty miles an hour. A cry of fury broke out from everyone. It was noon and we were no closer to catching the beast than we had been at eight o’clock.

Captain Farragut decided to fire the ship’s cannons at the beast. One shot hit the animal but slid into the sea without hurting it. I wished the creature would wear itself out, but hours passed without its showing any signs of exhaustion. I don’t know how far we traveled that day, but it must have been at least three hundred miles. Only darkness put an end to the chase.

At a little before eleven o’clock, the electric light reappeared about three miles away. Rocking gently on the surface, the narwhal seemed to be sleeping. The ship approached it cautiously to avoid waking it. Ned was ready with his harpoon. No one dared to breathe; we were only about a hundred feet from the bright light.

I saw Ned throw his harpoon and heard it strike a hard body. Suddenly the electric light went out, and two enormous gushes of water broke over the ship. Then the ship struck something and I was thrown over the railing and into the sea.

My plunge into the sea was so unexpected that I can't remember what I was thinking at the time. I'm a good swimmer, so I know I didn't panic. Once I was back at the surface, my first thought was to look for my ship. Had the crew seen me fall? Had the Abraham Lincoln turned around? Did I have any hope of being saved?
I caught a glimpse of a ship disappearing in the east, its lights dying out in the distance. It was the Abraham Lincoln ! I was doomed.
"Help! Help!" I shouted.
I swam desperately toward the ship, but my clothes made it difficult to move. I was sinking . . . I was suffocating!
"Help!"
That was my last cry before I started to slip below the waves. Suddenly a strong hand seized my clothes, and I felt myself being pulled to the surface. Then I heard these words in my ear:
"If you would kindly lean on my shoulder, you'll be able to swim more easily."
"Conseil!" I cried as I seized my faithful servant's arm. "Is that really you?"
"Yes, I'm here awaiting your orders," replied Conseil.
"That horrible collision threw you into the sea too?"
"No, but being your servant, I naturally followed you into the water."
"And what about the ship?" I asked.

Conseil flipped over to float on his back. "I don't think you should count on that ship to rescue you. When I threw myself into the water, I heard the man at the wheel say that both the rudder and propeller were broken."
"Broken?"
"Yes, broken by the monster's teeth. That's the only damage to the Abraham Lincoln , but it's bad news for us because they can't steer the ship anymore."
"Then we are lost!" I cried.
"Perhaps," Conseil replied calmly. "But we can survive for at least several hours more, and one can do a lot in several hours."

Conseil's unruffled calmness encouraged me, and I swam more vigorously. Since the Abraham Lincoln couldn't turn back to rescue us, our only hope was that Captain Farragut had sent out the small boats to search for us. We vowed to try to wait for as long as possible.

I decided that we should conserve our strength so that the two of us wouldn't be exhausted at the same time. Here's how we managed this: While one man floated on his back, the other man swam and pushed the floating man ahead of him. Taking turns for ten minutes at a time, we could swim for hours, perhaps until daybreak.

The Abraham Lincoln 's collision with the creature had taken place around eleven o'clock at night. I reckoned that we had eight hours to swim before sunrise, which we could do if we kept relieving each other. The sea was very calm, so that was in our favor.

But around one o'clock in the morning, I was overcome with terrible fatigue. My arms and legs were seized with horrible cramps. Conseil had to keep me afloat and our survival depended on him alone. I heard the poor fellow panting and I felt that he couldn't keep up this effort much longer.
"Leave me!" I said to him.
"Leave my master? Never," he replied. "I would rather drown."

Just then the moon appeared at the edge of a thick cloud. The surface of the sea glittered with its rays, and we felt revived. I scanned the horizon and spotted the Abraham Lincoln ! But there were no small boats on the water, and the ship appeared to be about five miles away.
My swollen lips could make no sound. Conseil could still speak, and periodically I heard him cry out for help. We stopped moving for a moment and listened.
"Did you hear that?" I murmured. "It sounded like someone answered you."
"Yes! Yes!" said Conseil, and he gave one more despairing call.
This time there was no mistake; a human voice had responded to Conseil's call. Was it another unfortunate victim who had fallen from the ship? Or was it a small boat hailing us in the darkness?
Leaning on my shoulder, Conseil raised himself half out of the water and then fell back exhausted.
"What did you see?" I asked.
"I saw . . . " he whispered. "I saw . . . But we shouldn't talk. We should save our strength."

Conseil was once more propelling me through the water. Sometimes he raised his head and uttered a cry that was answered by a voice that came nearer and nearer. I barely heard it. My strength was exhausted; my mouth opened and filled with salt water. I raised my head for the last time, and then I sank below the surface.
At this moment I struck a hard body. I clung to it, and then felt that I was being pulled up. I fainted. But I quickly came to because someone was trying to revive me.
"Conseil," I murmured as I half opened my eyes.
"Did you call me, Master?" asked Conseil.
But it was not Conseil who was vigorously rubbing my arms and legs. It was Ned Land.
"Ned!" I cried. "Were you thrown into the sea by the shock of the collision?"

"Yes, but fortunately I was able to quickly climb onto this island, or, perhaps I should say, climb onto our narwhal," replied the harpooner. "I soon discovered why my harpoon couldn't penetrate its skin."
"Why, Ned?" I said, thoroughly puzzled by this conversation.
"Because, Professor, the beast is made of sheet metal."
I sat up. The three of us were resting on top of something that was smooth and black.

Most of it was submerged below the surface of the water. I kicked my heels against our creature and heard a metallic sound in return. There was no doubt about it. This monster, this creature, this animal that had puzzled the world was man-made. Ned was convinced that we were lying on the back of a submarine, and Conseil and I could only agree with him.
Just then a bubbling began at the back of this strange thing, and the vessel began to move. We hung on for dear life.
"As long as it sails horizontally, I don't mind," muttered Ned. "But if it decides to dive, we're in trouble."

This long night continued to pass slowly. We clung to the strange vessel as it picked up speed. Several times I thought I heard some vague sounds coming from below us. It was almost as if someone had given a command and voices were responding. What kind of beings existed in this strange boat? I wondered. What was the source of its great speed?
Daybreak finally appeared. I was about to examine the hull upon which we rested when I felt the whole vessel starting to sink.
"Oh!" cried Ned, furiously kicking the metal beneath his feet. "Open up, you inhospitable rascals!"
The sinking movement stopped at once. We heard the sound of metal moving. An iron plate slid aside and a man popped up. He uttered a strange cry and immediately disappeared.
Moments later eight masked men appeared and silently forced the three of us into their strange machine.
Our abduction took place so quickly that I shivered all over. Who were our captors? They were undoubtedly some new sort of pirates, who explored the sea in their own way.

The narrow hatch closed above us and we were surrounded by complete darkness. My eyes, dazzled by the brightness outside the vessel, couldn't adjust to the lack of light inside. The men forced us down a metal ladder. At the bottom of the ladder, a door opened. We were shoved into a room and the door immediately shut behind us with a bang. The three of us were alone, and I couldn't even begin to imagine where we were. My eyes were still not able to discern even the faintest glimmer of light.
"These people are the worst hosts I've ever met!" shouted Ned. "Fortunately I still have my knife with me."
"Calm yourself, my friend," said Conseil.
"Yes, Ned," I said. "Don't make the situation worse with senseless violence. Perhaps we can get our captors to listen to us, but first let's try to figure out where we are."

I began to grope my way around the room. In five steps I came to a wall made of iron plates bolted together. Turning around, I ran into a wooden table around which were arranged several stools. The floor of this prison was concealed under thick mats that deadened the sound of footsteps. The bare walls revealed no trace of window or door. I guessed that the cabin measured about twenty feet by ten.

Half an hour had passed without any change in our situation when suddenly a bright light went on. I squeezed my eyes tight against the light. When I slowly opened them, I saw that the source of this brightness was an electric light in the ceiling. The sudden illumination of the cabin allowed me to examine it more carefully, but it only contained the table and five stools. We couldn't hear a sound; everything seemed dead onboard this mysterious vessel. Was it floating on the surface of the sea or had it dived into the ocean's depths? I had no idea.
But then we did hear a sound: the noise of bolts sliding. A door opened in a wall and two men appeared. One was short and very muscular with thick black hair and a mustache.

The second man was tall with a large forehead, straight nose, and fine teeth. One peculiar feature was that his cold, black eyes were set rather far apart. After observing him for a few moments, I decided that he was a calm, self-confident man full of energy and courage. But whether this man was thirty-five or fifty years of age, I could not say.

The two strangers wore fur caps and boots, and their clothes were made from a fabric that I couldn't identify. The taller man, who was evidently the captain of the vessel, carefully examined us in silence. Then he said something to his lieutenant in a language that I couldn't understand. The second man replied to him and stared at me as if waiting for me to speak. I said in French that I didn't know his language, but he didn't seem to understand me.
"Master, if you were to tell our story, perhaps these gentlemen might understand some words," suggested Conseil.

I began to describe our adventures onboard the Abraham Lincoln . Then I introduced us as Professor Pierre Aronnax, his servant Conseil, and Mr. Ned Land, the harpooner. The men listened to us quietly, but there was nothing in their faces to indicate that they'd understood a word.
"Perhaps they understand English," I said to Ned. "You speak it better than I do. Give it a try."

Once more Ned told our story in English, but with the same result. Next Conseil tried in German with no success. I even attempted to tell it in Latin. The two strangers exchanged some words in their unknown language and left the room.
Ned was furious. "We spoke to those rogues in French, English, German, and Latin, and they didn't have the politeness to answer!"
"Calm yourself, Ned," I said. "Anger won't do us any good."
"But don't you see, Professor? We'll die of hunger in this iron prison!" he replied.
"We won't starve," said Conseil calmly. "We can hold out for some time yet."
"My friends, we must not despair," I said. "Meanwhile I can't decide if our captors are from Spain, Turkey, Arabia, or India. Their language is quite incomprehensible."
As I said these words, the door opened and a steward entered with fresh clothes for us. While we hurried to dress, the steward set the table.
"Now that's more like it!" said Conseil.
"Bah!" said Ned. "What do you suppose they eat here—tortoise liver?"

The place settings were elegant and in perfect taste. We were undoubtedly dealing with civilized people, and if it weren't for the electric light, I could imagine we were dining in one of the finest hotels in Europe. All the dishes and silverware were inscribed with the letter N and a Latin motto: Mobilis in mobili .
"What does that mean, Professor?" asked Ned, running a finger over the letters.
" N is undoubtedly the captain's initial," I said. "And the inscription means mobile within the mobile element or in this case moving through water ."

We didn't talk much after that, being too busy devouring our food. I recognized some fish dishes, but I wasn't sure if some of the other things we ate were animals or vegetables. At least our hosts were not going to let us starve.

After eating, my two companions settled themselves on the floor of the cabin and were soon asleep. But I lay awake wondering where we were and with whom. At one point I thought the vessel was sinking to the bottom of the sea. Tormented by nightmares, I tossed and turned before finally falling into a deep sleep.

When I awoke I didn't know how long we'd been sleeping. We must have used up most of the air in the cabin because it was difficult to breathe. Just as I was speculating about how the captain refreshed the air for the whole vessel, I smelled a sea breeze. The ship rolled, and I realized that it had risen to the surface to breathe like a whale.
Ned and Conseil awoke and breathed in the pure, fresh air.
"What time is it?" asked Ned.
"I have no idea," I replied. "It's possible that we've slept for 24 hours."
More time passed and Ned grew angry. There was no sound on the boat, and it didn't move. I felt terrified; Conseil remained calm; Ned roared with anger and hunger.

Suddenly the door opened and the steward appeared. With a shout Ned threw the man to the floor. Conseil tried to pull Ned off the steward. I was just about to jump into the fray when I was stopped by hearing these words in French:
"Be quiet, Mr. Land, and you, Professor Aronnax, will you kindly listen to me?"

Startled, I turned around to see who had spoken to us in French. It was the captain of the vessel! Ned immediately released the steward, who tottered out of the cabin. Leaning against the corner of the table, the captain folded his arms and studied us with great care. Did he regret the words that he had just spoken? I wondered. For several moments there was silence, and none of us dared to break it.

"Gentlemen," the captain said in a calm and penetrating voice, "I am fluent in French, English, German, and Latin. Therefore I could have answered you earlier, but I wanted time to reflect. Each one of you told essentially the same story, so I believe you were telling the truth. I now know that you are Professor Pierre Aronnax of the Paris Museum of Natural History, his servant Conseil, and Ned Land, a Canadian harpooner aboard the U.S. Navy warship Abraham Lincoln ."
I bowed slightly to show that he was correct. The captain spoke French with perfect ease and without a trace of a foreign accent. Yet he didn't seem to be from France.

"No doubt you think that I've delayed a long time in paying you this second visit," the captain continued. "But I needed time to ponder my course of action toward you. Chance has brought you into the presence of a man who has cut all ties with humanity. Your arrival has disrupted my whole existence."
"Unintentionally!" I replied.

"Unintentionally?" replied the captain, raising his voice a little. "Was it unintentionally that the Abraham Lincoln chased me all over the Pacific? Was it unintentionally that you became a passenger on that warship? Was it unintentionally that your cannon balls rebounded off my vessel? Was it unintentionally that Ned Land struck it with his harpoon?"
I detected a restrained irritation in these words but knew that I had to respond.

"Sir, you are probably unaware that everyone in Europe and America is talking about your vessel," I said. "In pursuing you, those onboard the Abraham Lincoln believed that they were chasing a sea creature, a horrible monster that they had to destroy at any price."
The captain was not impressed with my explanation. "I'm sure that your warship would have been just as happy to destroy a submarine," he said.
I'm afraid that I agreed with him, but I didn't say that aloud.
"Therefore," he continued, "I'm within my rights to treat you as enemies. I could place you on top of this vessel and then sink below the waves, forgetting you ever existed."
"No civilized man would do that!" I protested.
"I'm not a civilized man. I have finished with society, for reasons that I alone know. Therefore I do not obey society's laws."
A flash of anger kindled in his eyes, and I had a glimpse of his terrible past. After a rather long silence, he went on.

"I've decided that there's a way to reconcile my pity for you with my own interests. You will remain onboard my vessel since fate has cast you here. You will be free, but in exchange for this liberty, I must impose one condition and you must swear to agree to it."
"What is that?" I asked.
"From time to time, I may have to confine you to your cabins for hours or even days," said the captain. "As I never want to use violence, I expect you to obey. Do you accept this condition?"
"We do," I replied. "But what do you mean when you say that we'll be free?"
"You'll be allowed to freely wander the submarine."
It dawned on me what this really meant. "Do you mean that we'll never see our friends and families again?"
"Yes, sir," replied the captain.
"What!" exclaimed Ned. "I can't swear that I'll never try to escape."
"But this is cruelty!" I cried.

"No, it's compassion," said the captain. "You are my prisoners of war, and I could throw you into the ocean depths if I wanted to. You attacked me and inadvertently found the secret of my whole existence. Do you think I'm going to send you back into the world with that secret? Never! In restraining you, it's not you that I guard but myself."
"So you are basically giving us a choice between life and death?" I asked.

"Yes." But then he went on in a gentler tone, "I know your work, Professor Aronnax. Your book on the mysteries of the seas is one of my favorites. You've done as good a job as you could from land, but you haven't seen nearly enough. You won't regret your time onboard my vessel because I'm about to embark on an underwater tour of the world."
I have to admit that this intrigued me, and for a moment I forgot that we were prisoners.
"By what name should we address you?" I asked.
"To you, I'm just Captain Nemo, and to me, you're just passengers on my submarine, the Nautilus ."
I smiled when the captain gave his name. Obviously he was intent on keeping his identity secret because nemo means "nobody" in Latin.
Captain Nemo called and a steward appeared. The captain gave the steward his orders in that strange language that I couldn't understand. Then he turned to Ned and Conseil.
"Follow the steward to your cabin, where breakfast is waiting," said Captain Nemo. "And now, Professor Aronnax, our meal is also ready. Permit me to show you the way."

He led me through a passage until we came to an elegant dining room. Tall oak cabinets stood at both ends of the room; their shelves were filled with china and glass of inestimable value. In the center of the room was a table spread with a fine meal. Captain Nemo indicated where I should sit.
I recognized some of the foods at this breakfast but not all of them. Captain Nemo seemed to read my thoughts.

"Most of these dishes are unknown to you," he said, "but they all come from the sea and you may eat them without fear. For a long time my crew and I have renounced food from the land, and we are healthy."
"Then where did you get this meat?" I pointed to one of the dishes.
"That which you believe to be meat, Professor, is really fillet of turtle. My chef is a clever fellow who excels at cooking the various products of the sea."
I ate while Captain Nemo entertained me with extraordinary stories.
"You like the sea, Captain?" I asked.
"Yes, I love it! The sea doesn't belong to tyrants. Upon its surface men can still wage war, but at thirty feet below the surface, their power disappears. Here I recognize no masters and I am free!"

Captain Nemo suddenly fell silent in the midst of his enthusiastic outpouring. Did he feel that he had said too much? For a few moments he paced up and down, much agitated. Then he grew calmer and his face recovered its usual icy composure.
"Now, Professor," he said, turning to me, "if you'd like to inspect the Nautilus , come this way."

A set of double doors opened at the rear of the dining room, and Captain Nemo led me into the next room. It was a library. Tall, black bookcases lined the walls, and they held a huge number of books. At the base of the bookcases were comfortable-looking couches covered in brown leather. In the center of the room stood an immense table littered with pamphlets and old newspapers.
Captain Nemo stretched out on a couch while I continued to admire his library.
"This library belongs in a fine European palace," I said. "I'm absolutely astounded when I consider that it's at the bottom of the sea."
"Where could one find greater solitude or silence than under the sea?" replied the captain. "Was your study at the museum as perfectly quiet as this?"
"No, sir. You must have six or seven thousand books here."

"Actually twelve thousand," said Captain Nemo. "I finished with the world on the day the Nautilus plunged beneath the waves for the first time. On that day I bought my last books and newspapers, and I like to think that people have written nothing more since then. Please feel free to make use of this library."

I began to examine the volumes on his shelves. With books in every language, his collection included works on science, ethics, and literature but nothing on politics or economics. By far the greatest number of books was about science. I saw a fairly new astronomy book that I knew had been published in 1864. From that, I concluded that the captain had been living underwater for at most three years.
"Come, let's continue our tour," said the captain, rising from the couch.

A door opened in the wall opposite where we had entered the room, and I followed Captain Nemo into a spacious room. The splendid lighting revealed that this room was a large gallery filled with treasures from the natural and artistic worlds.The walls were adorned with more than thirty paintings by some of the most famous artists of the past and present. The old masters were represented by Raphael, da Vinci, Rubens, and many others. In the corners of the room stood some admirable statues in marble and bronze.
"Sir," I said, "without seeking to know who you are, I recognize that you are an artist."

"No, merely a collector," said Captain Nemo. "I used to love to collect these beautiful works created by the hands of man. I greedily sought them out, and I've been able to bring together some objects of great value. But now they are my last reminders of a world that is dead to me."

He seemed to go into a daydream and forget that I was there, so I took the opportunity to study the rest of the room. The next thing I noticed was a large organ upon which were strewn works by Mozart, Beethoven, and other great musicians. In the center of the room was a fountain with a single stream of water that rose into the air. The base was made from a giant clamshell. Around this fountain stood elegant glass cases filled with wonders from the sea. You can imagine my interest in those.

One case was filled with coral, another with sponges. Yet another contained starfish, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers. Anyone interested in shells would have fainted at the sight of cases filled with so many rare and expensive specimens from around the globe.

Another case was devoted solely to pearls: pink pearls, green pearls, yellow, blue, and black pearls, the unusual production of diverse oysters from every ocean. Some of these pearls were larger than birds' eggs!

It was impossible to estimate the value of this collection. Captain Nemo must have spent millions to acquire these various natural specimens. I was wondering where his money came from when he interrupted my thoughts.
"You're examining my shells and pearls, Professor?" he said. "They must be of interest to a naturalist like yourself, but they have a special significance to me because I collected them all myself."

"No museum in Europe possesses such a collection," I said. "But if I exhaust all my admiration on it, I won't have any left for the Nautilus itself. I don't wish to pry into your secrets, but I confess I'd like to know more about the submarine. I see instruments hanging on these walls that I'm not familiar with."
"You'll find these same instruments in my own cabin, where I'll explain them to you," said the captain. "But first come look at your own cabin."

He led me out of the gallery, through a passage, and into my cabin, which was really too elegant to be called a cabin. It was furnished with a bed, table, and several other pieces of furniture. I found myself thanking my host.
"Your room adjoins mine, which opens into the gallery," Captain Nemo explained.

We entered the captain's room, which had a severe, almost monk-like appearance to it. There was only a small bed and a table—no comforts, only the strictest necessities. Captain Nemo pointed to a seat and I sat down. He explained that here and in the gallery, he had all the instruments that he needed to navigate the sub and keep track of the weather.
"But how do you power everything?" I asked.
"Ah," said Captain Nemo. "There is something that reigns supreme onboard my vessel: this agent lights the submarine, warms it, and is the soul of my mechanical apparatus. This agent is electricity."

"Electricity!" I cried in surprise. On land electricity was able to produce only limited amounts of power; it wasn't capable of powering such a fast and complicated vessel as the Nautilus . "But how are you able to do this? The batteries that you use to generate this marvelous force must be depleted very quickly."
"That's true, but my batteries are powered by sodium and someday I'll show you how we mine that."
"Do the batteries produce fresh air for the sub?" I asked.
"We could do that and we have some reservoirs filled with air, but I prefer to rise to the surface every day to replenish our air supply."
"Aha!" I said, for now I understood the sounds we'd heard onboard the Abraham Lincoln . The Nautilus really did rise to the surface of the ocean to breathe like a whale.

We continued our tour and the captain showed me the engine room and the kitchen. The door to the crew's quarters was closed, so I couldn't tell how many men were onboard. He also showed me a small boat that could be released from the sub for fishing or pleasure. But I was still filled with questions.
"How does the sub descend to great depths?" I asked. "How does it rise back to the surface? I hope I'm not asking too many questions."
"I don't mind answering," replied Captain Nemo. He stared at me for a moment before adding a grim reminder. "Because you'll never be able to leave the Nautilus to tell anyone what you've seen."
Captain Nemo and I returned to the gallery, where we settled ourselves on one of the couches. He showed me a set of drawings of the Nautilus .

"As you can see, Professor Aronnax," said the captain, "my ship is shaped like a cigar, measuring 232 feet in length and 26 feet at its widest point. It has two steel hulls joined together, which make it as strong as if it were made of solid metal."
"How does it sink under the water?" I asked, studying the plans.

"The submarine has reservoirs that can be filled with seawater when we need to descend," he explained. "But we don't have to take on a huge amount of water because everything has a natural tendency to sink in water."
"Then how do you make the submarine rise to the surface?"

"All we have to do is pump out the extra water," said the captain. "The pumps, which run on electricity, are very powerful. But I'm sure you observed that when jets of water burst over the Abraham Lincoln ."
I remembered that quite well.
"The submarine also has rudders on either side that help to guide it up or down," the captain went on.
"But how can the pilot see where he's going?" I asked.
"He sits in a glass pilot house on top of the vessel. Behind him is a powerful electric light that shows him the way."
"Aha!" I said. "That explains the glow of the 'narwhal' that puzzled us so. Well, Captain, your Nautilus is certainly a marvelous vessel."
"It is indeed, Professor, and I love it as if it were a part of myself. I am the engineer, builder, and captain of this wonderful boat."
"But how did you manage to build it in secret?" I asked.

"Each part came from a different place," said Captain Nemo. "The keel was made in France, the propeller in Scotland, the engine in Prussia, and the instruments in New York. I gave a different name to every supplier, so that no one could trace the orders back to me."
"Yes, but someone had to put the various parts together," I said, still mystified.
"I set up my workshop on a desert island. There my crew, whom I had trained, put the Nautilus together under my direction. When we finished, we burned all traces of our work."
I couldn't begin to imagine how much this vessel was worth, especially considering the value of the treasures onboard.
"One last question, Captain Nemo," I said. "Are you rich?"
"Immensely rich, Professor. I could pay the national debt of France and never miss the money."
I stared at him. Was he pulling my leg? Time would tell.
"Now," said Captain Nemo, "it's almost noon. Time for us to figure out our location and determine our starting point for this voyage. We need to go back up to the surface."
The captain pressed a button three times. The pumps began to drive the water from the tanks; the needle on one of his instruments showed that we were rising to the surface. The needle stopped moving.
"We've arrived," said the captain, who then led the way to a platform on top of the submarine.

The platform was only three feet above the water. Toward the middle of the platform I saw the slight bump that indicated where the small boat was stored. I also observed the two glass enclosures that the captain had described, one for the pilot and the other for the electric light that guided him.

The sea was beautiful and the sky was clear. A light breeze rippled the surface of the water. There was nothing in sight. Captain Nemo used his sextant to measure the altitude of the sun, thus determining our latitude.
"It's noon," said the captain. "Professor, whenever you're ready . . ." He indicated the hatch that led to the submarine's interior.

I took one last look at the sea and climbed down the ladder. I felt the vessel beginning to descend. In the gallery Captain Nemo used another instrument to calculate our longitude and determine our exact position on the sea.

"Our voyage under the seas began at noon today, November 8," he said. "We are headed northeast at a depth of 156 feet. Here are some maps upon which you can follow our course." He bowed to me. "And now I'll leave you to your studies."

I spent the next hour thinking about Captain Nemo and his amazing submarine. Then I noticed a large map on the table, and I put my finger on the spot where our voyage had begun. I realized that we were following the Black River, a powerful ocean current like the Gulf Stream. I was still staring at the map when Ned and Conseil appeared at the door of the gallery. They were standing still, frozen at the sight of the wonders spread before them.
"Where are we?" cried Ned. "In a museum in Quebec?"
"No, it must be a museum in Paris," insisted Conseil.
I motioned for them to enter. "My friends, you are in neither Canada nor France but onboard the Nautilus , 156 feet below sea level."
"Professor Aronnax," said Ned, "can you tell me how many men are onboard with us? Ten, twenty, fifty, a hundred?"

"I don't know," I replied. "I think you should give up any idea of seizing the Nautilus or escaping from it right now. This ship is a masterpiece of modern industry, and I'm glad I have the chance to see it. So be quiet for a while and let's see what happens."
"See!" exclaimed Ned. "But we can see nothing in this underwater prison! We're sailing blindly!"
Ned had barely said these words when all the lights went out. The three of us didn't dare to speak; we didn't know what would happen next. We heard something that sounded like panels sliding.
"It's the end!" cried Ned.
Suddenly light appeared at either end of the gallery, thanks to two large windows. The sea was clearly visible for a mile around the Nautilus . What a spectacle!
"Well, you wished to see, Ned," I said. "Now you can see."
"Amazing! Truly amazing!" muttered the harpooner, forgetting his bad mood.

Conseil was equally captivated by the view through the windows. As Ned named the fish, Conseil put them into their scientific classifications. I won't mention all the varieties that passed before my dazzled eyes for two hours, but they represented a superb collection of specimens that I had only read about. These fish, more numerous than the birds of the air, were undoubtedly attracted by the brilliance of the submarine's electric light.

Suddenly there was light in the gallery, the panels closed, and the enchanting vision disappeared. I expected Captain Nemo to join us, but he didn't appear. Ned and Conseil returned to their cabin, and I returned to mine, where I found that my dinner was ready.
I passed the evening reading, writing, and thinking. That night I slept deeply while the Nautilus glided rapidly through the current of the Black River.
The next day I awoke after sleeping for twelve hours. As usual Conseil came to my room to see if I needed anything.
"Did you sleep well?" he asked as he did every day when we were living on land.
"Quite well," I replied. "Where's Ned?"
"Still sleeping, Master. Ned appears to have plenty of practice at sleeping. He sleeps so soundly that I . . ."
Conseil chattered on, but I didn't respond because I was thinking about Captain Nemo. Why hadn't we seen him last night? I was sure he'd make an appearance today.

As soon as I was dressed, I went into the gallery. It was deserted. I plunged into studying the shells in the glass cases. I also enjoyed the huge albums filled with rare marine plants. Even though the plants were dried, they retained their lovely colors.

The whole day passed without Captain Nemo honoring me with a visit. The panels in the museum room did not open. Perhaps he did not wish us to tire of the beautiful view. The Nautilus continued on its course, traveling at a depth ranging from 150 to 180 feet.

The next day, November 10, I didn't see a single member of the ship's crew. Ned and Conseil spent most of the day with me, and they were astonished at the inexplicable absence of the captain. Was this eccentric man ill? Had he changed his mind about how he was going to treat us?

But as Conseil pointed out, we were still free to roam the submarine and we were always provided with delicious and abundant food. Our host kept his part of the bargain, and we couldn't complain because this voyage really was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

Early the next morning, November 11, I could smell fresh sea air, so I knew that the Nautilus had risen to the surface. I went up on the platform, where I fully expected to meet Captain Nemo. It was six o'clock; the sky was cloudy and the sea was gray but calm. I saw no one except the pilot in his glass cage.

I inhaled the salt air with delight as the sun's rays gradually burned away the fog. I was admiring the sunrise when I heard someone climbing up to the platform. I turned, fully expecting to greet Captain Nemo. But it was only his second-in-command, his lieutenant, the other man that I'd met on our first day onboard the Nautilus . He climbed onto the platform without seeming to see me. Putting his telescope to his eye, he scanned the horizon with great attention. When he'd finished, he went to the hatch and called down, " Nautron respoc lorni virch ."

What these words meant I couldn't say, but I have remembered this sentence because he repeated it every day under the exact same conditions. Having uttered these words, Nemo's lieutenant descended through the hatch. I thought that the Nautilus was about to resume its underwater voyage, so I went down to my cabin.
Five days passed like this without any change in our situation. Every morning I mounted the platform. The same man said the same sentence in the same strange language. Captain Nemo did not appear.

I had made up my mind that I would never see him again. But on November 16, I returned to my cabin with Ned and Conseil and found an envelope on my table. I opened it impatiently and read a note in bold, clear handwriting. The note was worded as follows:
To Professor Aronnax onboard the Nautilus:

Captain Nemo invites Professor Aronnax to a hunting party that will take place tomorrow morning in his forests on the island of Crespo. The captain hopes that nothing will prevent the professor from being present. The professor's companions are also invited to join the hunt.
Captain Nemo, commander of the Nautilus
"A hunt!" exclaimed Ned.
"And in his forests on the island of Crespo!" added Conseil.
"So it sounds like the captain is going ashore," said Ned.
I read the note again. "It certainly does seem that way," I said.
"Well, we must definitely accept this invitation," said Ned. "All this fish is fine, but I wouldn't mind eating some fresh venison."
I was still trying to make sense of Captain Nemo's invitation. He planned to go hunting in a forest yet had a strong aversion to anything on land.
"I've never heard of this island," I said. "Let's find out where it is."
I consulted the map and showed my companions a tiny island lost in the middle of the northern Pacific. I also noted that we were about 800 leagues from our starting point.
"If Captain Nemo sometimes does go on dry land," I said, "he certainly chooses remote islands."
The rest of the day passed without another word or visit from the captain.

When I awoke the next morning, I could feel that the Nautilus was perfectly still. I dressed quickly and entered the gallery, where I found Captain Nemo. He made no reference to his absence for the past eight days, but simply asked if we would be accompanying him today.
"We will," I replied. "But I'm puzzled by one thing: How can you own forests on Crespo Island if you've cut all ties with land?"
"My forests don't bask in the heat and light of the sun," he replied. "They aren't on land; they're actual underwater forests."
"You're offering to take me to real underwater forests?" I couldn't believe it.
"Yes, Professor, and without getting your feet wet. Now come eat breakfast with me. There aren't any restaurants on Crespo, and it will be a long time before you have supper."
While we ate, I asked the captain some questions.

"I'm familiar with a diving apparatus that lets a man breathe underwater, but he must stay tethered to a ship," I began. "Then there's a diving suit that allows a man to leave the ship, but it only contains a limited amount of air in a backpack. Which one will we be using?"
"A version of the diving suit," said Captain Nemo. "I've improved it so that a man can stay underwater for nine or ten hours."
"But how will we be able to see in the dark waters? And a regular gun won't fire in the water."
The captain smiled. "Don't worry. I've invented both a light and a gun that will work underwater. Are you ready to go hunting?"
We left the dining room and as we passed my companions' cabin, I called for them to join us. Near the engine room we came to a small room where we found a dozen diving suits.
"Oh no," said Ned. "I'm not getting into one of those."
"But there's no alternative," I said. "The forests of Crespo are underwater."
"Underwater?" Ned seemed to realize that his dream of eating venison was slipping away. "Unless someone forces me, I won't be going with you," the harpooner replied firmly.
"No one will force you, Mr. Land," said Captain Nemo.
"Are you coming with us?" I asked Conseil.
"I follow my master wherever he goes," replied my loyal servant.

Two members of the submarine’s crew helped us to dress for our underwater walk. Our diving suits were made of heavy rubber and constructed to resist the great pressure of the water. Each suit consisted of a jacket and trousers joined together with bands of copper crossing the chest. The sleeves ended in gloves that allowed the fingers to move easily. The trousers were finished off with thick boots weighted with heavy lead.

Captain Nemo, one of his crew, Conseil, and I were soon dressed. The upper part of the diving suit ended in a copper collar upon which was screwed a metal helmet. Three holes, protected by thick glass, allowed us to see in all directions. I was relieved to find that I could breathe with ease once the apparatus was turned on.
Our diving suits were so heavy that it was difficult to walk. Fortunately we only had to take a few steps into another small room. Then the door closed and we were wrapped in profound darkness.

After a few minutes, I heard a loud hissing and felt cold rising from my feet to my chest. Evidently water was entering the room. When the room was full of water, another door opened in the side of the submarine and we stepped onto the sea bottom!

How can I explain what it was like to walk underwater? Mere words are insufficient. I was astonished by how bright it was. Would you believe me if I said that at a depth of thirty feet I could see as if in broad daylight? The sun’s rays touched flowers, rocks, plants, and shells, providing a perfect kaleidoscope of colors: red, green, yellow, orange, purple, and blue. I wanted to share my amazement with Conseil, but underwater there was no way to communicate with him.

Soon the nature of the soil changed from sand to slimy mud. Then we traveled over a plain of algae that was as soft as any carpet woven by man. After a while the ground began to slope downward. The colors were no longer as brilliant, but we had no need of our lights yet. When we reached a depth of about three hundred feet, Captain Nemo signaled for us to stop. He pointed to a dark mass looming in the shadows.
"This must be the forest of Crespo," I thought and I was right. As the captain had said, the forest was underwater. There was no sign of an island.

Captain Nemo regarded this forest as his own. And who would have challenged his possession of this underwater real estate? What other pioneer would come, hatchet in hand, to cut down these dark masses of plant life? The forest was composed of large plants that resembled trees. I was struck by the unusual position of their branches, something that I had never observed before. No herb that carpeted the ground or branch that adorned a tree extended horizontally. They all stretched up to the surface of the ocean as straight as iron bars. I soon grew used to this strange fact as well as to the growing darkness that surrounded us. The soil of the forest was covered with sharp rocks that were difficult to avoid, and it was hard to tell the plants from the animals. It was still impossible to speak and be heard, so I put my great copper head next to Conseil’s. His eyes were shining with delight.

After a couple hours of walking underwater, I was surprised that I wasn’t terribly hungry. Instead I felt an overwhelming desire to sleep, something that happens to all divers. We all stretched out for a nap.

I don’t know how long I stayed asleep, but when I awoke, Captain Nemo had already risen. I was starting to stretch my limbs when something startled me and I jumped to my feet. A few steps away a giant sea spider, thirty-eight inches high, was watching me and was ready to spring. Although my diving suit was thick enough to protect me from this animal, I couldn’t help shuddering with horror.

At this moment Conseil and the other sailor from the Nautilus awoke, and Captain Nemo pointed out the hideous crustacean. He knocked the creature over with his gun, and I saw its horrible claws. This incident made me aware that we might encounter even more fearful animals—creatures whose attacks might penetrate my diving suit. I hadn’t thought of this before, but I resolved to be on my guard.

I was sure that our resting spot would mark the end of our walk, but Captain Nemo pressed on. We continued going downhill until we reached a depth of 450 feet and it got very dark. I had no instruments to measure this depth, but I knew that the sun’s rays couldn’t penetrate even the clearest water at 450 feet. We turned on our lights and could see ahead of us.

Captain Nemo kept plunging into the depths of the forest, whose trees were getting scarcer at every step. I was sure that our lights would draw some deep-sea dweller from its dark bed. But if sea creatures did approach us, they kept a respectful distance. Several times Captain Nemo raised his gun to his shoulder, but then dropped it and walked on.

At last this marvelous excursion came to an end when we reached a wall of solid rock. There was no way to climb it. We had reached the base of the island of Crespo, and Captain Nemo would not venture onto land.

We returned home by a different, steeper route. As we reached shallower waters, the captain shot a sea otter and his companion brought down a bird that was hovering above the waves. Off in the distance I spotted the bright light from the Nautilus ; we would be onboard in less than twenty minutes. I could tell that my air supply was beginning to run low on oxygen.

Suddenly Captain Nemo rushed toward me and pushed me to the ground. His companion did the same thing to Conseil. I didn’t know what to think of this unexpected attack, but I was reassured by seeing the captain lie down beside me and remain motionless.

I was stretched on the ground just under the shelter of an algae bush when I saw an enormous mass glide overhead. My blood froze in my veins as I recognized two giant sharks passing over us. They were blue sharks—an especially fierce kind of shark that could crush a man with their iron jaws! Happily for us, these hungry creatures couldn’t see well. They passed without spotting us even though they brushed us with their fins. By some miracle, we managed to escape a danger greater than meeting a tiger face-to-face!

In a few minutes, we were back at the Nautilus . I don’t know whether Conseil had classified the sharks as they swam over us. All I know is that I had observed them more as a potential victim than as a naturalist.

By the next morning, November 18, I had recovered from our adventures of the previous day. I went up on the platform, where Captain Nemo soon appeared and began a series of observations with his instruments. Meanwhile some sailors came up to haul in the fishing nets they'd laid the previous night. Although they appeared to be Europeans, they all used that strange language, so I couldn't determine their nationalities.
Nemo suddenly began speaking to me. "Professor, isn't this ocean like a living being? It has its moods. Last night it slept and now it has awoken after a quiet night."
When Captain Nemo spoke like this, he seemed like a different man.
"I can imagine," he went on, "clusters of submarine houses that would rise every morning to breathe like the Nautilus . Free towns, independent cities. Yet who knows whether some tyrant—"
Captain Nemo interrupted himself with a violent gesture. Our conversation was over without my having said a word.

During the weeks that followed, I seldom saw him, and when I did, he felt no need to explain his absence. His lieutenant regularly marked the submarine's course on the map, so I always knew where we were. By November 27 we had traveled 4,860 leagues and reached Hawaii. On December 1 we crossed the equator. From December 4 to 11, we traveled an additional 925 leagues. We passed December 25 without celebrating Christmas, much to Ned's regret.
Early on the morning of January 1, 1868, Conseil joined me on the platform.
"Master, may I wish you a Happy New Year?" he asked.

"I thank you for your good wishes," I said. "But I must ask what you mean by a 'happy' year in this situation. Do you mean a year that will bring us to the end of our imprisonment or a year that sees us continue on this strange voyage?"

"I don't really know how to answer, Master. We're sure to see some interesting things if we continue with Captain Nemo. In the past two months we haven't had time to be bored; the latest marvel is always the most astonishing. So I'd say a happy year would be one where we could see everything—"
"Everything, Conseil? No year could be that long. But what does Ned Land think about all this?"
"Ned's thoughts are exactly the opposite of mine," said Conseil. "He's tired of staring at fish through the windows and eating them at every meal."
"Oh, I don't mind the food," I said.

"Neither do I," replied Conseil. "I think as much about staying as Ned does about escaping. So no matter what happens, one of us will be happy. In conclusion I wish for you to have whatever will make you happy."
We shook hands and Conseil descended into the submarine.

By the next day, January 2, we had traveled 5,250 leagues under the sea. Over the next two days, we crossed the Coral Sea, and on January 4, we sighted the coast of New Guinea. On that day Captain Nemo announced that he intended to get to the Indian Ocean by the Torres Strait between New Guinea and Australia. Filled with coral reefs, it was a route that even the boldest navigators feared, and many considered the world's most dangerous strait.

The passage is about seventy miles wide, but it's obstructed by countless islands, islets, and rocks. It's almost impossible to navigate, so Captain Nemo had to take every precaution. Rising to the surface, the Nautilus proceeded slowly through the water. My two companions and I took advantage of the situation and climbed to the deserted platform. I suspected that Captain Nemo was piloting the sub himself. Around the Nautilus the sea appeared to boil as waves broke over the coral.
"This is a rough sea," said Ned. "I hope the captain knows what he's doing."
Indeed the situation was dangerous, but the Nautilus seemed to glide through the water like magic.

At about three in the afternoon, we were only a couple miles away from the island of Gilboa. Suddenly I was knocked off my feet—we had run aground! The Nautilus had just touched the coral below, but the vessel was now listing slightly to its portside.
When I stood up, I saw that Captain Nemo and his lieutenant were on the platform. They were examining the situation and talking in their incomprehensible language.

Unfortunately we had run aground in a part of the ocean where the tides were not strong. It would be difficult for the tide to rise high enough to float the sub off the coral. I was thinking about this when the captain, cool and calm as ever, approached me.
"An accident?" I asked.
"No, an incident," he replied.
"But an incident that may oblige you to become an inhabitant of land once more?"
Captain Nemo shook his head as if to say that nothing could force him to set foot on dry land again.

"The Nautilus is not damaged, Professor. It will still carry you into the midst of the ocean's marvels," he replied. "Our voyage has only begun, and I would not want to be deprived so soon of the honor of your company."
"But the tides aren't very high here," I said.
"That is true, but in five days, the moon will be full, so the tide will be at its highest. I fully expect the moon to take care of this incident for me."
Having said that, Captain Nemo and his lieutenant went back into the interior of the submarine. Once they were gone, Ned and Conseil approached me.
"Well, sir?" asked Ned. "What did Captain Nemo have to say?"
I explained how the captain said we must wait for the full moon to do its work.
"Really?" said Ned skeptically. "We're just going to sit here?"
"The captain is not going to do anything to try and move the Nautilus ?" asked Conseil.
"That is correct," I said.

Ned looked at Conseil and then shrugged his shoulders. "Sir, believe me, this hunk of metal is never going to navigate the sea again. It's only fit to be sold for scrap, therefore, I think it's time to part company with Captain Nemo."
I still had faith in the captain and his vessel, so I counseled Ned to stay put. "Flight might be possible if we were in sight of the English or French coasts, but out here—"
"Couldn't we at least go ashore?" asked Ned. "There are likely to be animals roaming the island, and I'm sure they could be turned into fine roasts and cutlets."
"Master, I agree with Ned," said Conseil. "Couldn't you ask your friend, Captain Nemo, to put us ashore, if only so we don't forget how to walk on land?"
"I'll ask, but I know he'll refuse."

To my great surprise, the captain agreed to our request. He didn't even make us promise to return, probably knowing that fleeing across New Guinea would be perilous. I'd decided that if Ned asked me about escaping, I'd say it was better to be a prisoner onboard the Nautilus than to fall into the hands of the natives.

At eight o'clock the next morning, we released the small boat from its hiding place atop the Nautilus . The sea was fairly calm. With Conseil and me rowing, Ned steered us safely past the coral reef that surrounded the island of Gilboa.

I was overwhelmed at setting foot on land again. Ned strode across the sand as if he were an explorer taking possession of the island. It was hard to believe that only two months had passed since we had become "passengers onboard the Nautilus " in Captain Nemo's words. In reality we were prisoners of the submarine's commander.

Within a few minutes we had plunged into a deep forest. While I was impressed by the beautiful mimosa and hibiscus flowers, Ned concentrated on getting something to eat. He discovered a coconut palm and retrieved some of the fruit. After he broke open a coconut with his hatchet, we drank the milk and ate the meat with gusto.
"Excellent!" proclaimed Ned.
"Exquisite!" said Conseil.
