"Professor, I don't think that Captain Nemo would object to our bringing some coconuts onboard the Nautilus , do you?" said Ned.
"I don't think he'd mind," I said, "but he won't taste them because they come from the land."
"Too bad for him," said Conseil.
"And all the better for us because there will be more for us to eat," said Ned.
"I have only one note of caution," I said as Ned began to attack another coconut tree.

"Coconuts are delicious, but before filling our boat with them, let's explore and see if this island produces any other useful things. Fresh vegetables would be a welcome addition to our diet onboard the Nautilus ."

"You are right," said Conseil. "I propose that we save three spaces on our little boat: one for fruits, one for vegetables, and one for meat. And speaking of meat, I have yet to see even the smallest example of an animal on this island."
"Conseil, you must be patient," said Ned.

For two hours we walked through the forest until we came upon a grove of breadfruit trees. Ned was familiar with the breadfruit, having eaten it during his numerous voyages. He became very excited at the sight of it.
"Professor, I will die if I don't taste some of this breadfruit right now," said Ned.
"Taste as much as you want," I said. "We're here to explore the island and the food it provides."
"It won't take long," Ned promised.
While Conseil and I gathered breadfruit, Ned got a fire going. Conseil brought a dozen breadfruit to Ned, who cut them into thick slices.
"You will see how good this is, Professor," said Ned. "Have you ever eaten it before?"
"No, Ned." I wasn't sure that I would like it.
"Well then, prepare yourself for something delicious. If you don't come back for more, then I'm no longer the king of the harpooners."

After a few minutes, the part of the fruit that was exposed to the fire was completely roasted. The interior looked like a white pastry, and I must confess that Ned was right. It was absolutely delicious, and I ate it with great enthusiasm.

We continued to travel through the forest, gathering bananas, pineapples, beans, and yams. At five o'clock we loaded our small boat and rowed away from shore. As we pulled up next to the Nautilus , no one came to greet us. The black hull seemed deserted. We loaded our provisions onboard and returned to our cabins, where we found supper waiting.

The next morning there was nothing new onboard, no sign of life. Our small boat rested where we had left it next to the submarine. Again we rowed out to the island. Ned hoped to have better luck with regard to hunting, so we decided to visit another part of the island.
After crossing a large prairie, we came to a small forest filled with brightly colored birds.
"These are only small birds," said Conseil in a disappointed tone.
"Yes, but they can be eaten if you're hungry enough," said Ned.
We decided to keep walking and soon came across some larger, more beautiful birds.
"Birds of paradise!" I exclaimed as the birds took off in undulating flight.

We must have used half our ammunition trying to bring one down, but we were unsuccessful. Hunger drove us on. Finally Conseil shot two pigeons for our breakfast. While the birds roasted, Ned prepared some breadfruit.
"These birds are excellent," he said, "but they are only side dishes. I won't be happy until I get some cutlets."
I knew that I wouldn't be happy until I got a bird of paradise—not to eat but to keep for my collection.

After eating we continued walking. Some harmless snakes glided out of our path. Birds of paradise fled at our approach and I despaired at ever getting one. But Conseil, who was walking ahead of me, suddenly uttered a cry of triumph and held up a magnificent specimen.
"Bravo, Conseil!" I cried. "If only I could bring this bird back to Paris and display it at the zoo in the botanical garden. How did you ever manage to catch it?"
"If you examine the bird, you will see that I don't deserve any credit. This bird has been eating nutmeg, which has made it quite drunk and easy to catch."

No sooner did I get my wish, than Ned got his: a large hog. We spent the rest of the day exploring the island, and Ned also managed to shoot some small kangaroos. By six o'clock we were back at the beach. Our small boat was still there and the Nautilus looked like a long rock emerging from the waves two miles away.

Ned quickly got down to the business of preparing supper. The hog, grilling on the coals, soon scented the air with a delicious smell. We had an excellent supper. Besides the hog, we dined on pigeons, breadfruit, mangoes, pineapples, and coconut milk.
"Suppose we don't return to the Nautilus tonight?" said Conseil.
"Suppose we never return?" added Ned.
Just then a stone fell at our feet and cut short the conversation.
My hand stopped in the midst of putting food into my mouth. We scanned the edge of the forest without moving but didn't see anything.
"Stones don't fall from the sky unless they're meteorites," observed Conseil.
A second stone knocked the pigeon's leg from Conseil's hand, proving him right. All three of us stood up and shouldered our guns, ready to answer any attack.
"Maybe it was just an ape?" suggested Ned.
"No, look." Conseil pointed toward the woods. "Natives."
About twenty natives, armed with slingshots and bows and arrows, appeared on the edge of the woods. They were only about a hundred feet from us.
"To the boat!" I cried.
Our boat was moored about sixty feet away. We started running as fast as we could while stones and arrows fell thickly around us.
"Hurry up, Ned!" I shouted as stones and arrows continued to rain down on us while we fled.

Ned couldn't stand to leave his provisions behind, so he tucked the hog and kangaroos under his arms and ran as fast as he could. In an instant the three of us loaded the boat, pushed it out to sea, and started rowing.
"That was close," said Ned, mopping his brow. "But at least they didn't get our food."

We hadn't gone more than five hundred feet when a hundred natives appeared on the shore, yelling and gesturing in a hostile manner. They rushed into the water up to their waists. I watched to see if the noise would draw some men from the Nautilus to the platform. But no. The enormous submarine lying offshore appeared completely deserted.
Twenty minutes later we were onboard the Nautilus again. I rushed to the gallery, where Captain Nemo was playing the organ.
"Captain!" I said, but he didn't hear me. I touched his hand.
He started and turned around. "Ah, Professor! Did you have a good hunt?"
"Yes, but I'm afraid we've been pursued by some hostile natives."
"Really?" Captain Nemo turned back to his keyboard, more interested in that than in my story. "How many do you think were after you?"
"At least a hundred."
The captain began to play again. "I wouldn't worry, Professor. All the natives of New Guinea could assemble on this shore, and the Nautilus would have nothing to fear."

The captain's confidence persuaded me, and I went to bed that night without any dread of the natives. The sub's hatches were open, so the natives could have easily slipped into the interior of the submarine. But they must have been frightened by the sight of the long, dark monster aground in their bay.

At six o'clock the next morning, I returned to the platform. The natives had taken advantage of low tide to come out on the coral. There must have been five or six hundred of them within several hundred feet of the sub. Nearly all of them were armed with bows, arrows, and shields, and they carried nets over their shoulders containing stones. The women wore grass skirts while some of the chiefs wore necklaces of red and white glass beads. One chief examined the Nautilus attentively. He was probably a man of high rank because he was draped in a mat of banana leaves set off with brilliant colors.

During low tide the natives roamed near the Nautilus , but they weren't troublesome. They frequently gestured to me and repeated a phrase as if they were inviting me to go onshore. I declined to do so. When the tide rose at eleven o'clock, they went back on land. I noticed that now there were even more of them on the island.

Having nothing to do, I called for Conseil to bring me a net. We spent the next two hours dragging for shells but found nothing unusual. But then when I least expected it, I put my hand on a rare specimen.
"Conseil, look at this!" I cried, holding up the shell.
"Oh, you have found something special indeed!" replied Conseil as he took the shell from my hand.

Conseil and I were absorbed in studying the valuable shell when a stone broke the precious object in Conseil's hand. I uttered a cry of despair while Conseil picked up his gun and fired at a native who was still holding a slingshot. Conseil's shot broke a bracelet of amulets encircling the man's arm.
"Conseil!" I cried. "No shell—not even a valuable one—is worth a man's life!"
"The scoundrel!" snapped Conseil. "I wish he'd shattered my shoulder instead. Let's start the attack."

I strongly disagreed. We were still discussing the matter when I looked up and saw that twenty canoes had surrounded the sub. Suddenly a shower of arrows hit the sub, and Conseil and I fled down the hatch.
I went to the gallery but found no one there, so I knocked on the door of the captain's cabin.
"Come in," he said.
I entered and found Captain Nemo in the midst of some complicated mathematical calculations.
"I'm disturbing you," I said politely.
"That is true, Professor," Captain Nemo replied, "but you must have a serious reason for doing so."
"Yes, sir. The natives have surrounded us with their canoes and in a few minutes they will certainly attack us!"

"Well, then we must close all the hatches." Captain Nemo pressed a button to transmit an order to the crew. "You don't think their arrows could have any effect on the Nautilus, do you, Professor?" he asked me. "Remember, cannonballs from the Abraham Lincoln failed to pierce it."
"No, sir. But I worry that the natives will get into the sub tomorrow morning when you open the hatches to take in fresh air."

"Let them come in. I see no reason to stop them, and I don't want my visit here to cost the life of even one native," said Captain Nemo. "By the way, Professor, we'll be departing tomorrow afternoon at exactly 2:40."
He bowed and I knew he was dismissing me, so I returned to my cabin. That night I had trouble sleeping because the natives were stomping on the platform and uttering deafening cries.

When I woke up the next morning, I could tell that the air had been renewed. The natives were still up on the platform, so Captain Nemo must have released some air from the reservoirs instead of opening the hatches. I worked in my room all morning without seeing Captain Nemo or seeing any evidence that we would be departing.

At 2:30 I went into the gallery; in only ten more minutes it would be high tide. If Captain Nemo were right, the Nautilus would soon be afloat once more; if not, we would be stuck here for who knows how long. I felt some vibrations as the ship's keel grated against the coral.
At 2:35 Captain Nemo entered the gallery.
"We're going to start," he said. "I've given the order to open the hatches."
"And the natives?" I said.
"What about them?"
"Won't they climb inside the Nautilus once the hatches are open?"
"No. Follow me and see what happens."

Captain Nemo led the way to the central staircase. Ned and Conseil were there, watching as the crew members opened the hatch to the platform. Twenty fierce faces peered down at us. But the first native who placed his hand on the stair rail jumped back, screaming and holding his hand in pain.
Ned rushed onto the staircase and the moment he seized the railing with both hands, he fell to the ground.
"I've been struck by lightning!" he cried.

Now I understood what was going on. The railings were electrified wires, so anyone who touched them got a terrible shock. The natives made a hasty retreat; we went to Ned's aid; and Nautilus , lifted by the tide at exactly 2:40, moved away from the coral bed. Our speed increased, and we finally passed safely out of the dangerous Torres Strait.

We were headed west, toward the Indian Ocean, and the Nautilus was traveling quickly. Where would Captain Nemo's whim carry us next? Only time would tell. Every day we were charmed by some new marvel that we saw through the windows of the submarine. Ned kept trying to vary our diet by introducing some of the foods we had gathered on our island excursion. Aside from that, we no longer thought about life on land until something very strange happened.

On January 18, I went up to the platform to greet the day as was my habit. I waited for the lieutenant to call out his usual phrase, but this time the words were different. Almost immediately Captain Nemo appeared and scanned the horizon with his telescope. For some minutes he didn't move. Then he lowered his telescope and exchanged some words with his lieutenant, who appeared agitated. The captain, however, remained cool.

What had they seen with their telescopes? I looked carefully at the horizon but could see nothing. The Nautilus was hundreds of miles from the nearest shore. Pacing the platform, Captain Nemo gave the order for the submarine to speed up. Just then the lieutenant drew the captain's attention to something. Captain Nemo stopped pacing and studied the horizon again with his telescope.

I had to find out what they were looking at. I went to the gallery and retrieved a telescope that I often used. Back on the platform, I raised it to my eye, but as soon as I did that, the telescope was snatched away! I turned around to face Captain Nemo, but I almost didn't recognize him. His eyes flashed and his teeth were clenched. His whole body betrayed his anger. He did not move while my telescope rolled at his feet. Had I unwittingly discovered some secret that provoked this fit of anger? I quickly realized that I was not the object of his hatred because he wasn't looking at me. His gaze was fixed on some distant point of the horizon.
"Professor Aronnax," he said in a particularly commanding tone, "I now require you to honor your agreement with me."
"What do you mean?" I asked.
"You and your companions must be confined until I decide to release you."
"You're the captain," I said while looking steadily at him. "But may I ask you one question?"
"You may not."
It would have been useless to try to resist his order. I went down to the cabin occupied by Ned and Conseil and told them what the captain had said.

You can imagine Ned's reaction, but there was no time for argument. Four of the crew arrived and conducted us to that cell where we had spent our first night onboard the Nautilus . Ned tried to protest, but the door was shut in his face.
"Master, will you tell us what this all means?" asked Conseil.
I had no idea what was going on and could only think of the strange fear on Captain Nemo's face.
"Hello! What's this?" said Ned, interrupting my thoughts. "Breakfast! But it's only the regular ship's fare, none of my special treats from the island."
"I suggest we eat it," said Conseil, "because we don't know when we'll see our next meal."
We took our seats at the table and ate in silence. Just then the ceiling light went out, leaving us in total darkness.
"That's all right," said Ned. "I'm feeling sleepy anyway."

To my astonishment both he and Conseil were soon asleep. I was wondering why they were so drowsy when I felt myself becoming very tired. My eyes closed despite my efforts to keep them open. I began to suspect that our food had been drugged. Evidently Captain Nemo felt that imprisonment wasn't enough to conceal his actions from us. I heard the hatches shut and thought I felt the Nautilus descending below the surface. I fell into a deep sleep filled with nightmares.

The next morning I awoke with a clear head. To my great surprise, I was in my own room. My companions undoubtedly had been transferred to their cabin. I tried my door and it opened, so I was once again free to roam the submarine. I went up on the platform, where I met Ned and Conseil. Like me, they had been astonished at waking up in their own beds. The lieutenant came up and pronounced his usual phrase. There was no sign of Captain Nemo.
Later that afternoon I was busy working in the gallery when the captain appeared. I hoped he might give me some explanation for the previous day's events, but he said nothing. He looked very sad.
After a few minutes he said, "Professor, are you a doctor?"
I was surprised at the question. "Yes, I am. I practiced medicine for several years before I joined the museum."
"Then would you look at one of my men who is ill?"
"Certainly," I said, curious if this man's illness had anything to do with yesterday's mysterious happenings.

Captain Nemo led me to a cabin near the crew's quarters. On the bed lay a man who was not only seriously ill but also gravely wounded. His head was covered with a bandage, and when I unwrapped it, I found a devastating injury.
"What caused this wound?" I asked.
"Does it really matter? How is he doing?"
I hesitated to give my opinion, but Nemo reassured me that the man couldn't understand me if I spoke French.
"He'll be dead in two hours," I said. "Nothing can be done to save him."
I was surprised to see tears glistening in Captain Nemo's eyes. He said, "You may go now, Professor."
For the rest of the day I felt upset. I slept badly that night and thought I heard distant music that sounded like a funeral hymn.
The next morning Captain Nemo asked if my companions and I could go for another underwater walk. This time Ned decided to go with us because he regretted having missed our underwater hunt.

Accompanied by Captain Nemo and about a dozen crew members, we left the Nautilus . I recognized at once that we were in the middle of a kingdom made of coral. Four of the men were carrying an oblong-shaped object. After walking for about two hours, we came to an area where there was a coral cross surrounded by small mounds of coral. Obviously the cross and mounds were man-made. And then it occurred to me that we were in the middle of a cemetery. The oblong object was the body of the man who had died the previous night.
A grave was dug and the man was buried with great care and ceremony. Back onboard the Nautilus , I talked to Captain Nemo.
"That was the man who died last night," I said.
"Yes, now the coral will do its work and cover him for eternity." Nemo buried his face in his hands and tried to suppress a sob.
"Your dead sleep out of the reach of sharks," I said quietly.
"Yes, sir, of sharks and men," gravely replied the captain.

As we continued our journey, I thought about Captain Nemo and how he had prepared his own cemetery under the sea. Conseil believed the captain to be a misunderstood genius, who had taken refuge in his own underwater world. But I felt that this explained only one side of Captain Nemo's character. Yes, Nemo was trying to escape the world, but he was also using the Nautilus for some sort of revenge. Why else had we been locked in that cabin and drugged? Why had the captain knocked the telescope from my hand when I tried to look at the horizon? How had that poor crew member received his fatal wound? At that moment I had no answers to these questions.

We were crossing the waters of the Indian Ocean with the Nautilus cruising at a depth of three hundred to six hundred feet. On the morning of January 24, we passed Keeling Island, almost midway between Australia and Ceylon. Ned and I were enjoying the fresh air on the platform.

"When we reach India," said Ned, "we'll find civilization. There will be roads and railways as well as English, French, and Hindu villages. I'm sure we'd also find many of our fellow countrymen there." He looked at me. "Don't you think it's time for us to leave Captain Nemo?"

"No, no, Ned," I said firmly. "Let's ride it out, as you seafaring fellows say. The Nautilus seems to be going back toward Europe. After we arrive in home waters, we can consider an escape. Besides, I don't think Captain Nemo will allow us to go hunting on the shores of Ceylon or India."
"Well, sir, couldn't we manage it without his permission?" asked Ned.

I didn't answer Ned because I didn't want any arguments. Deep down I was determined to take advantage of the good fortune that had put me onboard the Nautilus . On Nemo's vessel I could learn so much about the underwater world!

The next day the ocean was entirely deserted. The Nautilus passed the day on the surface, churning the waves with its powerful propeller and looking like a giant whale. There was nothing on the horizon until about four o'clock when I spotted a steamship. It was visible for an instant before it disappeared; we were too low in the water for anyone to spot us.
When I mounted the platform on January 28, there was land in sight, and I noticed a range of mountains. Captain Nemo soon appeared with a map in his hand.

"You're looking at Ceylon," he said, showing me the map and pointing to a teardrop-shaped island south of India. "It's well known for the pearl fisheries. Would you like to visit one of them, Professor Aronnax?"
"Certainly, Captain."
"Well, that's easily accomplished, although it's probably too early in the year to see any fishermen at work."

We went down to the gallery, where the captain explained that every March, three hundred boats gathered in the Gulf of Mannar to harvest pearls. The fishermen regularly dived to a depth of forty feet with the help of a heavy stone clutched between their feet.
A rope kept them attached to a boat.
"Do you mean to tell me that the fishermen don't use diving suits?" I asked in disbelief.

"No, they still use this old method," replied the captain. "They spend an average of thirty seconds underwater. During that brief time, they quickly stuff their little nets with as many pearl oysters as they can. By the way, Professor, you aren't afraid of sharks, are you?"
"Sharks!" I exclaimed. The answer to that question seemed pretty obvious. Of course I was afraid of sharks!
"We may run into some of them tomorrow, and I think you'll find they're quite interesting," Captain Nemo remarked, and with that, he left the gallery.

I stayed there, envisioning monstrous sharks with their rows of huge teeth bearing down on me. How could the captain be so casual about exploring shark-infested waters? He acted as if we were just going for a walk in the woods!
At this moment Conseil and Ned entered the room, looking quite happy and excited.
"Captain Nemo has just given us a very pleasant invitation!" said Ned.
"If it's agreeable to you," said Conseil, "Captain Nemo has invited us to visit the magnificent Ceylon pearl fisheries tomorrow."
"Did he mention anything else we might see?" I asked cautiously.
"No, Master," said Conseil.
I concluded that Captain Nemo had neglected to tell my friends about the sharks.
"Would you give us some details about fishing for pearls?" asked Conseil.
"Yes," said Ned. "What exactly is a pearl anyway?"

I gestured for them to sit down. "To the poet, a pearl is seen as a tear of the sea. In the East, a pearl is a drop of dew solidified, and to women, it is a jewel to adorn their fingers, their necks, and their ears. For naturalists it is simply a secretion of the oyster."
"But how does the oyster produce a pearl?" asked Conseil.
"It all starts with a small, hard substance like a grain of sand. The oyster secretes layers of pearly matter around that substance year after year," I explained.
"Can more than one pearl be found in the same oyster?" asked Conseil.
"Oh yes. Some oysters are virtual treasure chests of pearls. I've heard of one oyster that contained one hundred and fifty sharks."
"One hundred and fifty sharks !" echoed Ned.
"Did I say 'sharks'?" I said hurriedly. "I meant to say one hundred and fifty pearls. 'Sharks' wouldn't make sense."
"Does the price of pearls vary according to their size?" asked Conseil.

"Not only according to their size," I replied, "but also according to their shape, their color, and their luster—the special glow that makes them so appealing to the eye. The most valuable pearls are white and generally round or oval. "The round ones are made into bracelets while the oval ones become pendants. Of lesser value are pearls of irregular shape. The smallest pearls, known as seed pearls, are often used in embroidery for church vestments."
"Is pearl fishing dangerous?" asked Conseil.
"Well . . ." I hesitated, remembering the sharks. "As long as certain precautions are taken . . ."
"The only risk seems to be swallowing some mouthfuls of seawater," Ned chimed in.
"Whatever you say, Ned." I tried to sound as casual as Captain Nemo. "By the way, are you afraid of sharks?"
"Me? A harpooner by profession?" scoffed Ned. "With a good harpoon, I'm not afraid of anything! You know, sir, sharks are not well made. They must roll over to seize you, and in that time—"
Ned had a way of saying "seize" that made my blood run cold.
"And what do you think of sharks, Conseil?" I was hoping my loyal servant would say he wanted nothing to do with them. Then I would be able to use that as an excuse to avoid this expedition.
"I will be frank, Master," said Conseil.
I waited on pins and needles for his answer.
"If you intend to face the sharks," said Conseil, "then I will face them with you."

The next morning I awoke before dawn in anticipation of our trip to the oyster fisheries. When Captain Nemo and I went up to the platform, Conseil and Ned were already there. We stepped into the small boat, which was rowed toward Mannar Island by four crew members. As the sun rose, Captain Nemo ordered the crew to drop the anchor and help us into our diving suits. Evidently no one from the Nautilus besides its captain was going with us.
"Where are our lights?" I asked Captain Nemo.
"The water is so shallow that there will be enough sunlight to see by," said the captain. "And lights might attract sharks."
At the mention of sharks, I shuddered. I looked to see if Conseil and Ned had overheard, but their diving helmets were already covering their heads and ears. "What about our guns?" I asked.
"No guns," said Captain Nemo, handing us each a dagger. I noticed that Ned was also carrying an enormous harpoon that he had brought from the submarine.

After putting on my copper helmet, I followed the captain and the others into the water. Fish swirled around our feet as we slowly walked down a gentle slope. Nemo had been right; there was enough sunlight to illuminate even the tiniest sea creatures.

After walking for about half an hour, we reached the oyster fisheries. Captain Nemo pointed to the enormous heap of oysters surrounding us, and I immediately realized that I was looking at millions of them! Ned filled a net with oysters as the captain walked on; he was intent on leading us into a large cave.

At first I could see nothing, but as my eyes gradually became accustomed to the darkness, I could see a huge object on the bottom of the cave. It was an oyster of extraordinary size, a giant mollusk almost eight feet wide. I estimated that it must weigh about six hundred pounds and that it would contain at least thirty pounds of meat.

The oyster's two shells were partially open. The captain inserted his dagger between the shells to prevent them from closing, and then he directed my attention to something within the oyster. There I saw a single pearl equal in size to a coconut. Its round shape and beautiful luster made it a jewel of incredible value. Carried away by my curiosity, I stretched out my hand to touch it, but the captain stopped me. He removed his dagger, and the two shells closed suddenly. I then understood his intentions. In leaving the pearl within the oyster, he was allowing it to grow slowly. Each year the secretions of the oyster would add new concentric circles, and the pearl would increase in size and value. At that moment I estimated that it was already worth a great fortune.

Our visit to this giant oyster came to an end. Captain Nemo led us out of the cave, and we walked slowly, stopping whenever we came upon something that caught our attention. For my part, I was no longer worried about the danger of sharks, something that my imagination had so ridiculously exaggerated. Conseil walked along next to me, and placing his huge copper helmet against mine, his eyes gave me a friendly greeting.
About ten minutes later Captain Nemo suddenly stopped. I assumed we were going to turn around and return to the small boat.

But he gestured for us to crouch beside him in a wide crevice in a rock. He pointed toward something in the water, a shadow sinking to the sea bottom about five yards from me. My fear of sharks instantly returned, but I had nothing to fear because this was no monster of the deep.

It was a man, a lone pearl fisherman who was starting his harvest early. Looking up, I could see the bottom of his canoe. He held a stone between his feet to help him descend more rapidly. The stone was attached to the canoe by a rope.
Reaching the sea bottom, he fell to his knees and filled his bag with oysters. Then he ascended back to his canoe, emptied his bag, pulled up his stone, and started all over again.

The diver did not see us because the rock hid us. As I watched him, I realized that he could not carry away more than ten oysters at a time. He had to pry each one from the bank to which they were attached. He was risking his life by diving, but how many of those oysters had no pearl in them?

I watched him closely for perhaps half an hour. Suddenly as he was kneeling on the seafloor, he made a gesture of terror and sprang toward the surface. A gigantic shadow appeared just above him—an enormous shark was advancing on the man with its jaws open!

I was paralyzed with horror. The creature shot toward the fisherman, who darted to one side to avoid the shark's fins. But he was not quick enough to avoid the creature's tail, which struck him on the chest and knocked him down.

The whole attack lasted only a few seconds. The shark circled around, and was preparing to attack again when Captain Nemo rose suddenly and walked toward the monster, ready for a face-to-face fight. The shark noticed its new enemy and made straight for the captain. A terrible battle ensued. The shark struck the captain and was about to attack him again when Ned suddenly rushed forward with his harpoon and killed the creature. I sighed with relief.

Ned helped the captain to his feet. Captain Nemo immediately went to the fisherman, quickly cut the cord that held him to the stone, picked up the man, and rose to the surface. Within a few seconds, the three of us followed Nemo to the fisherman's boat. Captain Nemo's first concern was to resuscitate the man, which I did not think was possible. But after the captain and Conseil worked on him for a few minutes, the man opened his eyes. Imagine his terror at seeing four large copper heads leaning over him! And what must the man have thought when Nemo pulled a bag of pearls from his diving suit and placed it in the man's hands? The fisherman accepted this gift from the sea with trembling hands. His wide eyes showed that he didn't know what to think of these strange creatures who had saved his life and given him a fortune.

At a sign from the captain, we returned to the water and were soon back at our own small boat. The captain's first action was to thank Ned for saving his life. I thought about how brave Captain Nemo was, and how he had rescued a fellow human, even though Nemo had fled from the human race. Nemo said some chilling things, but this strange man was not completely heartless.
When I mentioned this to him later, Captain Nemo said in a voice filled with emotion, "That fisherman is an inhabitant of an oppressed country, and I will always be a native of that same land."

During the day of January 29, the island of Ceylon disappeared from the horizon. I consulted the map in the gallery and found that we had traveled 7,500 leagues. When we rose to the surface the next day, there was no land in sight, and we were once again alone on the ocean.
"Where do you think we're headed now?" asked Ned, who had joined me on the platform.
"We're going wherever our captain's fancy takes us," I replied. "When I looked at our course on the map, we seemed headed toward the Persian Gulf."
"Captain Nemo's fancy won't take us very far," said Ned. "The Persian Gulf has no outlet. So if we do enter the Gulf, it won't be long before we have to turn around!"
"Very well, then we'll come out again and maybe we'll visit the Red Sea."

"The Red Sea!" scoffed Ned. "It's a dead end too. The Suez Canal isn't finished, and even if it were, the captain wouldn't risk taking his submarine through the canal's locks. No, the Red Sea is not the route that will take us back to Europe."
"Perhaps we will reenter the Indian Ocean and travel down the east coast of Africa until we reach the Cape of Good Hope."
"And then where will we go next?" Ned asked.

"Well, then we'll enter a section of the Atlantic Ocean that we're not yet familiar with." I could tell that Ned was getting tired of this journey under the sea, but I was still an enthusiastic traveler. "For my sake, I'll be sorry to see the end of a voyage that so few men have had the opportunity to make."
"Don't you realize, Professor?" asked Ned. "It will soon be three whole months that we've been imprisoned here?"
"No, Ned, I didn't realize that; in fact, I don't want to realize it. I don't keep track of every day and every hour."
"But when will our imprisonment come to an end?" Ned persisted.

"When it ends. Meanwhile there's nothing we can do about it. If you tell me someday that we have a good opportunity to escape, then I'll listen to you. But until then, there's no point in even discussing this anymore."
"Waiting and staying silent may be fine for you, but in my opinion, a life in prison is no life at all." And with that statement, Ned left me alone on the platform.

It turned out that we were headed for the Red Sea, which we reached on February 7. I don't know why Captain Nemo decided to enter this body of water, but I approved of his decision because we began traveling at a slower speed. This gave me plenty of opportunities to observe life below the sea as well as the ancient towns along its shores. I spent hours at the gallery windows, gazing at species of plants and animals that I had never seen before.
A couple days later, I was standing on the platform when Captain Nemo came up to take the ship's bearings.
"Well, Professor Aronnax, does the Red Sea please you? Have you observed the wonders it holds: schools of fish, groupings of sponges, forests of coral?"
"Yes, Captain, and the Nautilus is wonderful for conducting such a study. It is truly a marvelous boat!"
"It is marvelous and indestructible. Traveling on this submarine, we do not need to fear the terrible storms of the Red Sea, or its currents and sandbanks."
"Your boat is at least a century before its time." I continued with my praise. "How sad that the secret of this invention will die with its inventor."
Captain Nemo was silent for a few minutes.
"It's a pity I can't take you through the Suez Canal," he said at last. "But you'll be able to see the long jetty of Port Said the day after tomorrow, when we'll be in the Mediterranean Sea."

"We'll be in the Mediterranean Sea the day after tomorrow?" I exclaimed. I was surprised, even though by now nothing about the Nautilus should have surprised me. "We'll have to travel at a rapid speed if we are to round the Cape of Good Hope and reach the Mediterranean by then!"
"Who said that we would sail down the coast of Africa and around the Cape of Good Hope?" Captain Nemo replied.
"Well, unless the Nautilus sails on dry land and passes above the isthmus—"
"Or beneath it, Professor Aronnax," he interrupted me.
"Beneath it?" I echoed.

"That's right," replied Captain Nemo. "There is a subterranean passage that I have named the Arabian Tunnel. It takes us beneath the Suez and opens into the Mediterranean. Not only does this passage exist, but I have made use of it several times. Without it, I wouldn't have ventured into the Red Sea."
"But how did you find it?" I asked.
"A combination of luck and reasoning," he replied.

Captain Nemo then explained that he had noticed there were some identical species of fish in the Red Sea and the Mediterranean. He guessed that the subterranean current ran from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean because the Red Sea was higher. So he caught a large number of fish in the vicinity of Suez. He put a copper ring through their tails and threw them back into the Red Sea. A few months later he caught some of these fish in the eastern Mediterranean.
"I then looked for the tunnel with the Nautilus ," said the captain. "I passed through it, and the day after tomorrow, you will too."
On the night of February 11, the Nautilus remained underwater. According to my calculations, we must have been very near Suez.
"It can't be easy to pass through this tunnel of yours," I said to Captain Nemo as we sat in the gallery after supper.
"No, and for that reason I usually go into the pilothouse and steer the submarine myself. You're welcome to come with me."

We made our way to the pilothouse on top of the submarine. The cabin was dark, but soon I could see the pilot, a strong man who stood with his hands resting on the large wheel. Outside, the sea was brightly illuminated by the electric light behind the pilothouse.
"Now," Captain Nemo said. "Let's look for our passageway."
We traveled for almost an hour with Captain Nemo directing the pilot to make small changes in the submarine's course.
"There!" exclaimed Nemo as a passage, black and deep, finally opened before us.

The captain took the wheel and I heard the waters of the Red Sea roaring through the tunnel. On the walls of the narrow passage, I could see nothing but bright streaks from our electric light. Our engines churned the waves and the Nautilus went with the torrent, as swift as an arrow. My heart pounded furiously.
At last Captain Nemo handed the wheel back to the pilot and turned to me. "The Mediterranean!" he announced triumphantly.
Early the next morning Ned and Conseil joined me on the platform.
"Well, Sir Naturalist," said Ned, addressing me in a cheerful tone, "where are we today?"
"We're floating on the surface of the Mediterranean Sea," I replied.
"I don't believe that for one minute," said Ned. "We couldn't have crossed the Isthmus of Suez."
"If Master says it's true, then it must be true," said loyal Conseil.

"Thank you, Conseil." I described for them how the Nautilus had swiftly passed through Captain Nemo's underwater tunnel. "That shoreline over there is Egypt. You have such good eyes, Ned, that you can probably see the Port Said jetty stretching into the sea."
Ned looked in the direction I pointed. "Why, I believe you're correct, Professor. We are in the Mediterranean. Good! Now let's discuss our own business where no one will overhear us."
Ned led the way to a small space behind the electric light on top of the submarine.
"What I have to say is very simple," Ned began. "We're in Europe now. Before Captain Nemo's whims drag us back to the Pacific Ocean, I want to leave the Nautilus ."

I didn't want to be responsible for restricting the freedom of my companions, but I really had no desire to leave. Thanks to Captain Nemo and his submarine, I was rewriting my book on deep-sea life while living in the very midst of it. I didn't want to abandon the Nautilus before my research was finished.
"Ned, do you regret the time you've spent underwater?" I asked.
The harpooner paused for a moment before replying. Then he crossed his arms and said, "I don't regret it, but I want this voyage to end."
"I have to admit I don't know when that will be," I said. "But it will end."
"I agree with Master," said Conseil. "And it's possible that Captain Nemo will let us go after he has crossed every sea on earth."
"I don't think that will happen." I shook my head. "We know too much about the captain and his submarine for him to let us go. But in six months, perhaps we'll find another opportunity to escape."
"Six months!" exclaimed Ned. "Where on earth will we be in six months?"
"I don't know," I replied. "But whenever we decide to escape, we must succeed on our first attempt. If we fail, we'll never have another opportunity, and Captain Nemo will never forgive us."
Ned was still determined to escape as soon as possible. He outlined a plan that involved taking the small boat one night when we were along the European coastline.
"Do you want to know what I think of your plan?" I asked.
"Certainly, Professor Aronnax," said Ned.

"I think we'll never have the chance to escape because Captain Nemo will always be on guard, especially when we're near Europe." I stood up. "And now not another word on the subject. The day that you're ready to escape, let us know and we'll follow you. I leave everything up to you."

The next day we reached the Greek islands. I wanted to spend some time studying the marine life, but the panels in the gallery remained closed until evening. After supper Captain Nemo joined me in the gallery. He seemed preoccupied and didn't speak to me, but kept peering through the windows. Suddenly a man appeared in the water.
"Look, Captain!" I cried. "That poor man has been shipwrecked. We must save him!"

The captain didn't answer me, but leaned against the window. To my astonishment, the man in the water approached and pressed his face to the glass. Captain Nemo gave him a signal and the man headed for the surface.
"Don't worry about him," said Captain Nemo. "That's Nicholas, a bold diver who swims from one Greek island to the next. His nickname is 'The Fish.'"

Captain Nemo went over to a chest in a corner of the room. I could barely contain my shock as he opened it, revealing a supply of gold bars! He seemed to have forgotten I was there as he carefully counted the bars. There must have been two tons of gold in that chest. Where did he get it all and what was he going to do with it? I wondered.

The captain closed the chest and wrote an address on it in Greek. He pressed a button to communicate with the crew, and within a few minutes four men appeared. With great difficulty, they removed the heavy chest from the gallery.
Captain Nemo turned to me. "What were you saying, Professor?"
"I wasn't saying anything," I replied, still in shock at what I'd witnessed.
"Then I will bid you good night."

I returned to my cabin very puzzled about what I'd seen. I tried to fall asleep, but I kept wondering about the connection between the appearance of the diver and the removal of the chest filled with gold.
Soon I felt the rolling movements that signaled the Nautilus had risen to the surface. I heard steps upon the platform—someone was unfastening the small boat and launching it!
The boat struck the side of the submarine and then all was silent. Two hours later I heard the same noises and knew that the small boat had returned, and the Nautilus was sinking below the waves.
The next day I told Ned and Conseil about the strange events of the previous evening.
"How much do you think the gold is worth, Master?" asked Conseil.
"Where was the gold taken?" asked Ned.
I had no answer for either question, so I returned to working on my notes in the gallery. Around five o'clock I began to feel so hot that I took off my jacket.
"Perhaps I'm getting a fever?" I thought. I continued my work, but I kept feeling hotter and hotter.
"Could there be a fire onboard?" I asked myself.
I was about to leave the gallery to check when Captain Nemo entered. He went over to the thermometer.
"Forty-two degrees," he said.
"If it gets much hotter, we won't be able to stand it," I said.
"Oh, it won't get any hotter if we don't want it to. We can simply move away from the source that's producing this heat."
"So it's outside?" I was still puzzled.
"Yes, we're floating in a current of boiling water. Look!"
He opened the panels to reveal a white and boiling sea. "I wanted you to see the unusual spectacle of an underwater volcano."
I pressed my hand to a window, but the heat was so great that I sprang back. The Nautilus had stopped moving and the temperature in the room was unbearable.
"We can't stay one moment longer in this boiling water!" I cried.
"You're right," said Captain Nemo, as calm as ever.
He gave an order and the submarine turned around. Fifteen minutes later we were breathing fresh air on the surface.
That's when a startling thought occurred to me: if Ned had chosen this part of the Mediterranean for our escape, we never would have survived.

The Mediterranean Sea is bordered by orange trees and rugged mountains. The air is pure and perfumed with the scent of myrtle. But Captain Nemo was in a hurry, so I experienced none of the Mediterranean's enchantments. Starting from the shores of Greece on the morning of February 16, we traveled at full speed and reached the Atlantic Ocean 48 hours later.

It was obvious to me that Captain Nemo wanted to avoid the countries surrounding the Mediterranean. The breeze probably brought back too many memories, and perhaps too many regrets. We were traveling so quickly that Ned had to give up any hope of escape. It would have been impossible to launch the small boat when we were traveling thirty-five to forty feet per second. He might as well have jumped off a train going at full speed. I followed our route on the gallery map and calculated that we had traveled ten thousand leagues in three and a half months.

Later in the morning of February 18, the Nautilus rose to the surface, so we could take our daily walk upon the platform. I went up at once, accompanied by Ned and Conseil. But the Atlantic Ocean was so rough that the submarine rocked violently with every wave that crashed over it. We soon decided to go below. Conseil returned to his cabin while Ned followed me to mine. When my door was shut, he sat down and looked at me silently.
"Ned, my friend," I said, "I know how disappointed you must be that we couldn't escape while in the Mediterranean."
The harpooner did not respond, yet the crease in his brow and the expression on his face showed me that he was thinking hard.

"I don't think we should give up yet," I continued. "We're going up the coast of Portugal. France and England are not far away, and we can easily find refuge in one of those countries. Now if the Nautilus were traveling south, I'd share your uneasiness, but I think you'll be able to act in a few days."
Ned stared at me for a few more moments before he spoke. "We're leaving tonight."
I was so startled by this statement that words failed me.
"We agreed to wait for an opportunity," Ned went on, "and that opportunity has arrived. Tonight we'll be only a few miles from the Spanish coast. It's cloudy and windy—good conditions for an escape."
As I was still silent, Ned stood up and faced me.

"We leave tonight at nine o'clock," he said. "I've already told Conseil to be ready. At that time Captain Nemo will be in his room, probably asleep. Conseil and I will go up the central staircase, and you'll remain nearby in the library, awaiting my signal. The oars, mast, and sail are already in the small boat, and I've even gotten us some provisions. So everything is ready."
"But the sea is so rough," I said, finally finding my voice.

"I agree, but we have a sturdy boat and we'll be traveling only a few miles. Who knows where the Nautilus will be tomorrow? We could be hundreds of leagues away, so we have to take this chance tonight. I will see you later, at nine o'clock."

With these words Ned departed, leaving me feeling numb. I had always imagined that when the time came to escape, there would be an opportunity to discuss it. But Ned had given me no time to think, never mind talk, over the matter. I knew he was right; this was a good opportunity to escape. But it was still hard to believe that the moment had arrived.

At that point I heard the sounds that meant the submarine was sinking under the waves. I passed the rest of the day torn between the thrill of freedom and the sadness of abandoning my underwater studies. Sometimes I hoped our escape would succeed, and other times I wished something would happen to prevent us from leaving the submarine. Twice I went to the gallery to check if we had changed our course. But no. The Nautilus was still cruising up the coast of Portugal. This day of waiting seemed to last forever.

My supper was served in my room as usual, but I could eat little. At seven o'clock, there were still 120 minutes left. I couldn't sit quietly anymore so I went to see the gallery for the last time. I spent a long while admiring its treasures, and I wished the panels were open so I could gaze underwater one more time. A clock struck eight, startling me. I returned to my room and dressed warmly. I wasn't taking anything with me besides my notes.

At a few minutes before nine, I pressed my ear to the door that linked my cabin and the captain's. Silence. I returned to the gallery and then went to the library. I stood at the door leading to the central staircase and awaited Ned's signal. Suddenly I heard the submarine's propeller slow down and stop. The only sound came from my heart beating loudly. I felt a slight shock and knew that the Nautilus had stopped on the sea bottom. Something was not right and there was no signal from Ned.
"There you are!" Captain Nemo entered the library from the gallery. He was smiling broadly. "I've been looking all over for you, Professor. Do you know the history of Spain?"
"What?" I was still startled by the captain's arrival in the midst of my escape.

"I asked if you knew the history of Spain." Captain Nemo went on to describe a famous sea battle where Spanish ships, loaded with silver and gold, were sunk in 1702. "We're right at the shipwreck site. If you come with me, you'll likely be very interested in what I have to show you."

By this point, I'd recovered my composure, so I followed him into the gallery, where the panels were now open. I looked out and saw a shipwreck. Members of the submarine's crew were carrying silver and gold bars as well as precious jewels back to the Nautilus .
"This treasure, as well as other shipwrecks that I've marked on a map, are the source of my great wealth," Captain Nemo explained.
"But doesn't this all belong to someone?" I asked. "The Spanish government? And even if it doesn't, aren't there poor people who could benefit from all these riches?"
As soon as I spoke, I saw that I had wounded the captain.

"Do you think I collect these treasures for myself?" asked Captain Nemo. "Do you think I'm ignorant of all the suffering people on this earth, miserable creatures who should be consoled, victims who should be avenged?"

And then I understood for whom those gold bars in the Grecian islands were destined. My ruined escape plans seemed like such a small problem compared to the misery of those people who needed the captain's philanthropy.

21.title: A Visit to a Legendary Place

paragraphs.text: I was not surprised when Ned came to my cabin first thing the next morning. He looked very disappointed after our failed attempt at escape.
"Well, Ned," I said, trying to comfort him. "Luck was against us last night."
"I couldn't believe that the captain decided to stop the submarine at the very hour we intended to leave it."
"Yes, he had to do some business at his bank."
"His bank?" Ned gave me a curious look.
"Captain Nemo keeps his wealth under the ocean, where it's safer than in any bank vault."

I then told Ned everything that the captain had told me the previous evening. I also described all that I'd seen through the windows. I hoped my description of the captain's charity would persuade Ned not to abandon the submarine, but that was not the case.
"It's not over yet," he said. "Another time we'll succeed, and tonight if necessary—"
"What direction is the Nautilus heading?" I interrupted.
"I don't know," said Ned.
"We'll know for sure at noon when the lieutenant records our position on the map. Until then let's have no more talk of escape."

The harpooner returned to his cabin, and I went into the gallery. The compass was not reassuring if we intended to escape. The Nautilus seemed to be going southwest, which meant that we were turning our backs on Europe.

At about 11:30, the reservoirs were emptied, and the submarine rose to the surface. I rushed to the platform and found Ned already there. There was no land in sight, nothing but an immense sea. The air was foggy and the winds were whipping up. Ned kept trying to see through the thick fog, hoping that he'd spot some land, but there was nothing to see. At last he put down his telescope and ranted against Captain Nemo until the lieutenant came up to the platform.

An hour later we were sailing underwater again. I returned to the gallery and consulted our position on the map. We were now more than three hundred miles from the nearest shore. There was no way to escape, and Ned was enraged when I informed him of our situation. As for me, I wasn't especially sorry that we'd had to abandon our dangerous plot for now. Relieved of my anxiety, I was able to return to my work with some degree of calmness.
Late that night I received an unexpected visit from Captain Nemo.
"I propose an unusual excursion, Professor," he said. "So far you've visited the ocean's depths only by daylight. Would you like to see them at night?"
"Most certainly," I replied.
"I must warn you that it will be a tiring experience. We'll have to walk a good distance and climb a mountain. The underwater 'roads' are rather rough."
"You've only increased my curiosity with what you've said. I'm ready to follow you, Captain."

He led the way to the room where we usually put on our diving suits. I was surprised to see that none of the crew was coming with us, and Captain Nemo had not invited Ned or Conseil. As we put on our suits, I wondered aloud where our electric lights were.
"We won't need them," said Captain Nemo, "but you will need one of those." He pointed to a metal-tipped walking stick.
It was almost midnight when we set foot on the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean. The waters were very dark, but the captain pointed to a red light shining brightly about two miles away.

After a while the surface under our feet became slippery. I realized I was walking on seaweed-covered stones. My feet often slipped on this strange carpet, and I would have fallen more than once without my walking stick. As the rosy light that guided us grew brighter, I remained puzzled by it. Was I headed for some natural phenomenon that was unknown to man? Or was it made by man? Were we going to meet some friends of Captain Nemo who had also rejected living on land? I would not have been surprised to encounter one of those clusters of underwater houses that Captain Nemo had dreamed of.

It was one o'clock in the morning when we arrived at the bottom of the mountain. But first we had to struggle through a grove of dead trees. Then we began our climb of the mountain. We climbed over rocks and jumped over crevices. Two hours after leaving the Nautilus , we were still climbing. We came upon some massive rocks that sheltered deep caves. My blood curdled whenever I saw an enormous antenna blocking my path or a sharp claw snapping shut in the shadow of some cavity. Millions of small spots shone brightly in the dark. These were the eyes of giant lobsters and crabs crouched in their holes. Captain Nemo, more used to these creatures than I was, seemed unbothered, pushing on until we reached a plateau.

Below us lay some ruins, which to my surprise, looked as if they were made by man, not nature. There were vast heaps of stone among which I could definitely see the outlines of castles and temples. What was this? Where were we? I wanted to ask Captain Nemo, so I touched his arm, but he only pointed toward the mountain's peak.

In a few minutes we reached the top, and looking down, I realized that this mountain was an underwater volcano. The glowing red light was really lava, and there below us was a town that the volcano had destroyed. Its roofs were open to the sky, and its temples had fallen. Its columns were lying on the ground. It was like an underwater version of Pompeii.
I had to know where we were. I tried to speak, but Captain Nemo stopped me with a gesture. Picking up a chalk-like stone, he wrote one word on a black rock: Atlantis.

The legendary lost continent from ancient times! I tried to fix in my mind every detail of this grand landscape. Captain Nemo remained motionless, leaning on a mossy stone. Was he dreaming of a civilization long since disappeared? Was it here that he—a man who wanted no part of modern life—came to steep himself in history? I wished I had access to his thoughts!

At that moment the moon appeared above us and cast its pale rays on the buried continent. It was but a glimmer, but what an unbelievable sight! The captain stood up straight, took one last look over the ruins below us, and then signaled me to follow him.

We quickly descended the mountain. Once we passed through the grove of dead trees, I could see the electric light of the Nautilus shining like a star to guide us home. Captain Nemo walked straight toward the ship, and we were soon onboard. I went to sleep thinking of all the amazing things I'd seen.

I woke up very late the next morning. Tired from my visit to the lost continent of Atlantis, I slept until eleven o'clock. I dressed quickly and hurried to the gallery to learn where the Nautilus was heading. The instruments showed that it was still journeying southward at a speed of twenty miles per hour and a depth of three hundred feet.

I spent most of the day watching the fish through the windows in the gallery. Around four o'clock my view was blocked by a high wall. It must have been a continent, or at least an island—perhaps one of the Canary Islands or Cape Verde Islands off the African coast. At this point the panels closed, and I decided to take a nap.

I did not wake up until the following morning. I checked the instruments in the gallery and found that the Nautilus was floating on the surface of the water. But it was odd that I didn't feel any waves rocking the submarine. I heard footsteps on the platform, so I climbed as far as the hatch. To my surprise, when I looked up, I didn't see daylight. Instead we were surrounded by a deep darkness.
"Where are we?" I said out loud, though I didn't expect anyone to answer me. "Have I mistaken the time? Is it still night?"
I was surprised when a voice above me said, "Is that you, Professor?"
"Ah, Captain," I replied. "Where are we?"
"Underground."
"Underground!" I exclaimed. "How can the Nautilus be floating underground?"
"Wait a few minutes until our light is on, and you'll see."

I climbed up to the platform and waited. It was so dark that I couldn't even see Captain Nemo. But looking straight up, I perceived a dim light coming from a circular hole. At that moment the submarine's bright light came on, and I took the opportunity to look around. The Nautilus was still, floating on a circular lake that was two miles wide. This lake was imprisoned by walls that were five hundred yards high and slanted inward. At the top of the walls was the circular opening through which I could now see daylight.
"Where are we?" I asked the captain again.

"In the heart of an extinct volcano," he replied. "An earthquake caused the sea to invade it, and we entered through a natural canal that runs about thirty feet below the surface of the ocean. Show me any other harbor on earth that can offer such a perfect place of refuge."
"You're surely safe in here," I said, "but what use is this refuge to you? The Nautilus doesn't really need a port."
"No, though I like to think of this as our home port. What the Nautilus needs is electricity. We make electricity from sodium; we get sodium from coal; and we mine coal right here."
"So will I get to see your men mining coal?"

"No, we don't have time for that. I'm in a hurry to continue our voyage around the world. The men will be loading some sodium that we've stored here," said the captain. "But we'll only be here for one day, so if you want to explore the lake and the volcano's crater, you'll have to do it today."

I went in search of Ned and Conseil and found them in their cabin. I asked them to follow me up to the platform. Conseil, who was quite used to strange things, wasn't the least bit surprised to learn he'd woken up in the heart of an extinct volcano! Meanwhile Ned immediately began thinking of ways to find an exit from the volcano.
"We are once more on land," Conseil declared as we stepped onto a dock on the lake's shore.
"I don't call this land," said Ned grumpily, "and besides, we're not on land but under it."

We found a path that wound around the crater's walls. Some shrubs and even some trees grew from cracks in the walls. I noticed many beautiful, fragrant flowers and a variety of birds circled in the air above us.
We had arrived at the base of some sturdy trees when Ned exclaimed, "Look! A hive!"
"And there are bees humming around it!" said Conseil.
I approached the hive and found that they were correct. Naturally Ned wanted to gather some honey, and I couldn't object. He quickly made a small fire and smoked the bees out of their hive.
"When I have mixed this honey into some breadfruit," said Ned in a more cheerful voice, "I'll be able to offer you a delicious cake."
"It'll be as sweet as gingerbread!" said Conseil.

We climbed as close to the volcano's summit as we could with Ned trying unsuccessfully to capture some birds. When we returned to the dock, Captain Nemo's men were just finishing loading the sodium. The Nautilus could have left right then, but the captain did not give the order. I suspected that he wanted to wait until night so that no one would see us emerging from the secret entrance.

After that we continued on our journey and the Nautilus crossed the Sargasso Sea, which was filled with mats of seaweed. For the next nineteen days the submarine stayed in the middle of the Atlantic. There was no chance of escape. I hoped that once Captain Nemo had completed his trip around the world, he would let us leave if we swore never to tell a soul about him and his submarine. But a part of me knew that would never happen. During this time I rarely saw the captain, but I often found his books left open in the library. One day I even found that he'd been reading my book. He had made notes in the margins where he disagreed with my findings.
By this point it was March, and we had traveled thirteen thousand leagues. We had now reached a place where the Atlantic Ocean was supposed to be exceptionally deep.
"We're going to try to reach the sea bottom today," Captain Nemo announced one morning when he found me in the gallery.

He gave the orders and the Nautilus quickly began to descend. I could feel the submarine's steel plates shuddering as the water pressure increased. We passed the depths at which most fish could live and yet we continued to descend. Finally we reached the sea bottom at a depth of almost ten miles below the surface.
"Look at these magnificent black rocks, these uninhabited caves!" I exclaimed. "No living thing can survive here. Oh, how I wish I could always remember these fabulous sights!"
"You can," said the captain, and he called for a crew member to take a photograph for me.
"Now we must ascend," he continued. "I don't want to expose the Nautilus to this much pressure for too long. Hold on tight."

I was about to ask why, when I was suddenly thrown to the floor. The captain had signaled for the submarine to rise and we were shooting toward the surface. In a mere four minutes, the Nautilus emerged from the water like a flying fish.

I imagined that when we had traveled as far south as Cape Horn, we would turn west and head into the Pacific Ocean. But Captain Nemo did nothing of the kind. Instead he continued to head south. Was he going to the South Pole? That would be sheer madness.

In the meantime Ned had stopped mentioning his escape plans. I could see that our imprisonment was weighing upon him, and I could feel that rage was burning within him. When he met the captain, his eyes lit up with suppressed anger. I feared he might do something that he would later regret.
On the morning of March 14, he and Conseil came to my cabin.
"I have one simple question for you, Professor," said Ned. "How many men do you think are onboard the Nautilus ?"

"I don't know, my friend," I replied. "Probably ten men would be enough to run it." I knew that Ned was thinking about how many men he'd have to overpower to take control of the submarine. "But you have to consider the other people too."
"What other people?" asked Ned.
"If my suspicions are correct, then the Nautilus houses more than just its crew. It also serves as a refuge for men like Captain Nemo who have cut all ties with land."

"Perhaps that's true, Master," said Conseil, "but this submarine can hold only a limited number of men. You know the size of the vessel and the amount of air it contains. You also know that the Nautilus must return to the surface every 24 hours to refresh its air supply. Can't you estimate the maximum number of men it could hold?"
I did some quick calculations. "There's enough air onboard to supply 625 men for 24 hours, but I can't imagine there are more than 60 men onboard."
"That's still too many," said Conseil.
Ned simply shook his head and left my cabin without saying anything.

"Will you allow me to make one observation, Master?" asked Conseil. "We must try to understand how difficult it is for poor Ned because there's nothing for him to do here. He's not as interested in the wonders of the sea as we are."
"I agree, Conseil. The monotony of life onboard must seem intolerable to him after a life of freedom and activity."

Ned rarely reacted to anything at sea, but later that morning something happened that seemed to spark a change in him. The three of us were sitting on the platform, relaxing in the fine weather. The seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere, which meant we were experiencing fall at a time when we normally enjoyed spring in Europe.
Suddenly Ned jumped up and shouted, "A whale!"
"So," I teased him, "you haven't lost your ability to spot whales after all these months!"

"Never, Professor. Once a whaler, always a whaler. Why, I believe there are ten whales out there. No, wait, twenty! And I can't go after them because I'm stuck on this confounded vessel." Ned pounded his fist on the railing, but his eyes looked brighter than they had in weeks.
From that point on, the Nautilus remained on the surface of the ocean, and we soon began to see floating pieces of ice about twenty to twenty-five feet long.

We passed even larger pieces and finally encountered actual icebergs. Ned had fished in the Arctic, so he was familiar with its icebergs, but Conseil and I admired this natural phenomenon for the first time. Some of these icebergs were streaked with green; others resembled enormous amethysts with the light shining through them.

The farther south we went, the more these floating islands increased both in number and size. The ice took surprising forms, sometimes resembling a Middle Eastern town with mosques and minarets, and then, a city tumbled to the ground by an earthquake.
No matter where we were, Captain Nemo always managed to find a small trail of blue water for us to follow. One day the ice completely blocked our passage, but this didn't stop the captain.

The Nautilus entered the brittle ice like a wedge and split it with a frightful cracking sound. Violent gales struck us and every part of the submarine was covered with ice. We traveled on until about two o'clock when, despite all the captain's efforts, the Nautilus could proceed no farther.
We couldn't go backward either because every opening had closed behind us. I was on the platform with Captain Nemo when we became trapped in the ice.
"Well, Professor, what do you think of this?" he asked.
I wanted to say that I thought he'd been very unwise to get us into this situation, but I restrained myself. Instead I said, "I think we're stuck, Captain."
"So you don't think the Nautilus can free itself?"
"I think it'll be difficult because winter is coming, and the ice won't be breaking up for a long time."
"Oh, Professor, you always see nothing but obstacles and trouble. I swear to you that the Nautilus will free itself—and then travel all the way to the South Pole!"
"To the South Pole?" I thought in surprise. No one had ever reached the South Pole.
"I will not fail," said the captain as if he were reading my thoughts. "We'll discover it together, you and I."
"Sure," I said sarcastically. "There are no obstacles for us. Let's blow up this iceberg, and if that fails, let's give the Nautilus wings to fly over it!"

"No, not over it but under it," said Captain Nemo. "As I'm sure you know, most of an iceberg is underwater, but that won't hinder us because we can go still deeper. The only problem is that we must come to the surface for fresh air."
"Yes, but the Nautilus is equipped with a metal battering ram on its bow. If you attack the ice on a diagonal, perhaps the shock would cause it to break up."
"Now you're thinking like an optimist!" The captain smiled.

The preparations for this daring attempt now began. Air was pumped into the submarine's reservoirs while ten men climbed along the sides of the Nautilus . Armed with pickaxes, they broke up the ice around the vessel, which was soon free. We went below and the submarine began to descend.

Once underwater, we traveled at such high speed that I calculated we would reach the South Pole in forty hours. For most of the night, the novelty of the situation kept us at the gallery windows, but around two o'clock, I went to bed. I had not seen Captain Nemo since our conversation, but I assumed he was in the pilothouse.
The next morning I returned to the gallery, where the instruments told me that the submarine was slowly ascending. My heart beat very quickly. Were we going to emerge and return to open waters?
No! A second later a huge shock told me that the Nautilus had struck the bottom of an iceberg, a huge one, judging from the deafening sound.
Several times that day the submarine tried to rise again, and every time it struck the ice, which lay like a thick, impenetrable ceiling above it.

That night there was little change in our situation; we were still under five hundred feet of ice. During the night I woke up several times and found that we were slowly rising to the surface as the layer of ice above us grew thinner. Finally, at six o'clock in the morning, Captain Nemo came to the door of the gallery.
"The sea is open," was all he said before quickly departing, but that was enough for me.
I went up to the platform, where the captain was looking at the water; it was still crowded with pieces of ice and moving icebergs.
"Are we at the South Pole?" I asked.
"I don't know," he replied. "I'll take our bearings at noon to determine our location."

Captain Nemo invited my companions and me to join him when he set foot on land, but only Conseil and I were interested. Two crew members rowed us to shore in the small boat. Conseil was about to jump out when I held him back.
"Sir," I said to Captain Nemo, "the honor of being first to set foot on land belongs to you."
"Thank you," said the captain. He climbed out of the boat, and after a few minutes said to us, "Whenever you like . . ."

We followed him onto the rocky shore, where we observed seals and penguins. Unfortunately, it was too foggy to see the sun and take our bearings, so we were still not sure about where we had landed. We returned to the submarine, disappointed but hoping to have better luck the next day. Unfortunately the following morning, our view of the sun was once again obscured, this time by heavy snow.
Finally, on the third day, Captain Nemo led us toward a peak, where we watched the sun burst through the clouds. He made his observations and confirmed that we were at the South Pole.
"I, Captain Nemo, have reached the South Pole today, March 21, 1868, and I take possession of this part of the globe," he said gravely.
"In the name of which monarch?" I asked, remembering how an explorer usually claimed land on behalf of his ruler.
"In my own name!" replied Captain Nemo, holding up a black flag bearing a gold N.

The next morning, at six o'clock, the crew of the Nautilus prepared to leave the South Pole. With its reservoirs filling with water, the submarine began its slow descent. At one thousand feet below the surface, it headed north at a steady 15 miles per hour. Toward night it was already floating under an immense iceberg.

At three o'clock in the morning, I was awakened by a violent shock. I sat up in bed and was thrown into the middle of the room by another shock. The Nautilus , having struck something, had rebounded and hit something else. I rushed to the gallery, where I found the furniture overturned. I heard footsteps and excited voices, but Captain Nemo did not appear. As I was leaving the gallery, Ned and Conseil entered.
"What's going on?" I asked them.
"That's what I came to ask you, Master," said Conseil.
Ned scowled. "The Nautilus has run aground. Judging from the way it's lying, I doubt it'll right itself as it did in the Torres Strait."
"So, do you think we're at the surface?" asked Conseil.
"That's easy enough to find out." I consulted the instruments, and to my great surprise, I discovered that we were more than a thousand feet underwater. "We must speak to Captain Nemo."

The three of us went in search of the captain, but when we couldn't find him, I decided he must be in the pilothouse. We returned to the gallery to wait for him. After about twenty minutes, the captain entered the room, but he took no notice of us. His normally emotionless face showed signs of unease. He watched the compass silently and then read the other instruments. I didn't want to interrupt him, but when he turned toward me, I decided to speak.
"An incident, Captain?" I asked, using the phrase he'd preferred in the Torres Strait.
"No, Professor, it's an accident."
"Serious?"'
"Perhaps," he replied. "We've run aground underwater, but we aren't in immediate danger."
"May I ask, sir, what caused this accident?"
"An enormous block of ice, an entire iceberg, turned over and slid under the Nautilus ."

Captain Nemo said that the submarine was now emptying its reservoirs in an attempt to right itself, but the block of ice was rising with it. He explained this while never taking his eyes from the instruments.

Suddenly we felt a small movement below us; evidently the submarine was righting itself slightly. Ten long minutes passed while we watched the pictures on the wall slowly return to their normal position and the floor become horizontal under our feet.
"Are we floating again?" I asked.
"Of course," replied the captain, "but we're still underwater."

I looked through the windows and saw that a dazzling wall of ice rose about ten yards away from either side of the Nautilus . There was also ice above and below us. We were imprisoned in a perfect tunnel of ice filled with water. But I decided it would be easy to escape the tunnel. The submarine could go either forward or backward and then dive under the iceberg.

Captain Nemo left us, and I assumed he returned to the pilothouse. My companions and I stayed at the gallery windows, dazzled by the submarine's light sparkling on the ice. At five in the morning, we felt a shock at the vessel's bow; its battering ram had obviously struck a block of ice.
"We must go in reverse now, and see if we can find another way out," I said, trying to appear cheerful.
"That'll take hours more," grumbled Ned. "How long are we going to be stuck here?"
I had no idea, so I went to the library to calm my nerves. I threw myself on a couch and tried to read a book. Fifteen minutes later Conseil and Ned entered the room.
"Is that an interesting book, Master?" asked Conseil.
"Very interesting," I replied.
"Well, it should be." Conseil laughed. "It's the one you wrote!"
I slammed the book shut, and the two of them turned to go. I stood up.
"Let's return to the gallery," I said. "We should stay together until we're out of this predicament."
"As you wish, Master," replied Conseil.

Several hours passed while the Nautilus moved backward at a good rate of speed, and we kept an eye on the instruments. It was almost 8:30 when we felt another shock, this time at the stern. I turned pale and seized Conseil's hand. The three of us exchanged troubled glances. At this point Captain Nemo entered the room.
"The iceberg has shifted and closed up every outlet," he announced.
Once again we were trapped in the ice!
We were imprisoned in the tunnel of ice. Ned banged the table with his fist. Conseil stayed quiet while I watched the captain. Once again Nemo's face betrayed no emotion.

"Gentlemen," said Captain Nemo, "there are two ways of dying in this situation." He made these remarks as calmly as a mathematics professor lecturing his pupils would. "The first is to be crushed by the ice, and the second is to run out of air."
"We don't have to worry about running out of air, do we?" I asked. "Our reservoirs are full."

"We have spent the last day underwater and already the submarine's air needs to be renewed. Obviously we can't get to the surface to refresh the air, and in two days—maybe three—we will have exhausted the supply in our reservoirs."
"Well, Captain, can we get out of this situation by then?" I asked.
"We will certainly try," he replied. "I'm going to run the Nautilus aground on the iceberg below us. My men will then put on their diving suits and attack the ice wherever it's the thinnest."
Captain Nemo left the gallery, and the submarine soon began to sink slowly.
"My friends," I said to Conseil and Ned, "we're in serious trouble here, but I rely on your courage and good spirits."
"Professor," replied Ned, "I'm as handy with a pickax as I am with a harpoon, so if I can be useful to the captain, I'm willing to help him."
"He won't refuse your aid," I said. "Come with me, Ned."

I led him to the room where Captain Nemo and some crewmen were putting on their diving suits. I told the captain of Ned's offer, which the captain accepted. When Ned was dressed, I returned to the gallery and found Conseil looking out the windows. A few minutes later we saw a dozen men set foot on the ice. Captain Nemo drilled holes in the ice to determine where it was the thinnest, and then the men attacked the ice with their pickaxes.

After two hours of hard work, Ned came in, exhausted. He and his comrades were replaced by new workers, including Conseil and me. The submarine's crew worked for twelve hours and managed to clear away only a small patch of ice. At this rate it would take us at least four days to get out of the tunnel.
"And even if we do get out of this infernal prison," said Ned, "don't forget that we're still under the iceberg. Who knows how long it will be until we reach open water and can rise to the surface!"
When I went out to work the next morning, it seemed as if the walls of the tunnel were starting to close in on us. I didn't say anything to Ned or Conseil, but I did mention it later to the captain.
"I'm aware of that," he replied, as calm as ever. "It's one more danger, but the only thing to do is remove the ice faster than it is building up on the tunnel walls."
